items.title: Web Development at MHSM
items.text: This site contains the course notes and exercises for the web development program at Makerere High School Migadde. You will learn how to structure pages with HTML, style them with CSS, and later add behaviour with JavaScript.

items.title: Start here
items.text:
1. Read Elements and Page Structure. It explains the parts of an HTML element and the skeleton every page needs.
  2. Create a folder for your work and add a file called index.html.
  3. Open that file in a browser. Keep the editor and the browser open side by side, change something, save, and reload.

If you can see a heading and a paragraph in the browser, you are ready to continue.

items.title: What you need
items.text:
• A plain text editor. Notepad, TextEdit, VS Code, or any editor that saves plain text will work.
  • A modern browser such as Firefox, Chrome, Edge, or Safari.
  • A folder where you can keep your practice files.

You do not need an account, a framework, or a build tool for the HTML and CSS chapters.

items.title: HTML
items.text: Structure and meaning. You will mark up headings, paragraphs, links, images, lists, tables, forms, and page sections.

items.title: CSS
items.text: Presentation. You will link a stylesheet and learn how to control colour, spacing, type, layout, and responsive behaviour.

items.title: JavaScript
items.text: Not available yet. The JavaScript page explains what is planned. Finish the HTML and CSS tracks first.

items.title: How to use the notes
items.text:
• Work through the chapters in order the first time. Later chapters assume you have seen the earlier ones.
  • Type the examples yourself instead of copying them. You will remember the mistakes you fix.
  • Do the short practice tasks. Reading code is not the same as writing it.
  • Use the navigation at the end of each page. It follows the order of the course.

items.title: When something does not work
items.text:
The page is blank. Check that the file ends in .html and that you opened the file you just saved.

The tags appear as text. Check the file extension. A file named index.txt will show the markup instead of rendering it.

The styles do not apply. Check that the stylesheet is in the same folder as the HTML file and that the href matches its name exactly.

The browser still shows the old version. Save the file, then reload the page. If that fails, clear the cache or open the file again.

items.title: HTML Course
items.text:
HTML describes what each part of a page is: a heading, a paragraph, a link, a table, or a form field. This track starts with the structure of a single element and ends with a complete page made from semantic sections.

You do not need any previous HTML experience. Work through the chapters in order.

Start with Elements and Page Structure

items.title: Getting started
items.text:
• Elements and Page Structure: tags, elements, attributes, nesting, and the page skeleton.
  • Headings: how to outline a page and why one <h1> is enough.
  • Heading Levels: a quick reference for <h1> to <h6> with practice.

items.title: Text
items.text:
• Paragraphs: how paragraphs, line breaks, and thematic breaks differ.
  • Text Blocks: the exact syntax for <p>, <br>, and <hr>.
  • Build Your First Page: put headings and paragraphs together in one page.
  • Emphasis and Meaning: choose between <strong>, <b>, <em>, <i>, and <mark>.
  • Code and Technical Text: mark up code, keyboard keys, program output, and variables.
  • Small Semantic Tags: abbreviations, dates, edits, subscripts, and superscripts.
  • Quotations: inline quotes, block quotes, and citing a source.
  • Address and Fine Print: contact information and secondary text.

items.title: Links, images, and lists
items.text:
• Links: link to pages, sections, email addresses, and other websites.
  • Images: image sources, alt text, dimensions, and captions.
  • Lists: unordered, ordered, nested, and description lists.

items.title: Data and input
items.text:
• Tables: rows, columns, headers, captions, and data that belongs in a table.
  • Forms: labels, inputs, buttons, and a complete registration form.

items.title: Page structure
items.text:
• Grouping Content: when to use <div>, <section>, and <span>.
  • Page Landmarks: <header>, <nav>, <main>, <footer>, <article>, and <aside>.

items.title: What you should be able to do at the end
items.text:
• Read an HTML file and explain what each element is for.
  • Build a page with a clear heading outline and correctly nested elements.
  • Add links, images, lists, tables, and forms.
  • Choose semantic elements instead of wrapping everything in <div>.
  • Check your own page for missing labels, alt text, and closing tags.

The CSS track uses the same pages and adds presentation. Continue there when you can build a simple HTML page without copying the examples.

items.title: Elements and Page Structure
items.text:
An HTML page is made from elements. An element tells the browser what a piece of content is, so a paragraph is marked as a paragraph and a heading is marked as a heading.

This chapter covers the parts of an element, how elements nest, and the skeleton that every HTML page needs.

items.title: Tags, content, and elements
items.text:
A paragraph looks like this:

<p>Fresh bread is baked every morning.</p>

It has three parts:

<p>                                  opening tag
Fresh bread is baked every morning.  content
</p>                                 closing tag

The opening tag names the element. The content sits between the tags. The closing tag has a forward slash and marks the end. All three together make the element.

Use lowercase element names. <P> usually works, but lowercase is easier to read and matches the rest of the examples.

items.title: Elements without closing tags
items.text:
Some elements do not wrap content, so they have no closing tag:

<img src="bread.jpg" alt="A loaf of bread">
<br>
<hr>
<input type="text">

These are called void elements. You may see a trailing slash such as <br /> in older code. HTML does not require it.

items.title: Elements that contain other elements
items.text:
Elements can contain other elements:

<p>
  This loaf is <strong>still warm</strong>.
</p>

The <strong> element sits inside the <p> element. This is called nesting. When you nest elements, close them in the reverse order you opened them:

<p>
  <strong>Correct</strong>
</p>

Do not cross the tags:

<p>
  <strong>Incorrect</p>
</strong>

The rule is: last opened, first closed.

items.title: Attributes
items.text:
An attribute gives the browser extra information about an element. Attributes go in the opening tag and usually have a value:

<a href="menu.html">See the menu</a>
  • href is the attribute name.
  • "menu.html" is the attribute value.
  • The value is written in quotes.

An element can have more than one attribute:

<img src="bread.jpg" alt="A loaf of bread" width="400" height="300">

Attribute names are lowercase by convention. Use double quotes and keep the value inside them.

items.title: The page skeleton
items.text:
Every page starts with the same basic structure:

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>MHSM Bakery</title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>MHSM Bakery</h1>
  <p>Fresh bread is baked every morning.</p>
</body>
</html>

Here is what each part does.

items.title: <!doctype html>
items.text: The doctype tells the browser to use standards mode. Put it on the first line, before anything else.

items.title: <html>
items.text:
The <html> element wraps the whole document. The lang attribute tells browsers and screen readers which language the page uses:

<html lang="en">

Use en for English. The closing </html> goes at the end of the file.

items.title: <head>
items.text:
The <head> contains information about the page. Most of it is not visible in the page body.

<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>MHSM Bakery</title>
</head>
  • <meta charset="utf-8"> lets the browser display characters such as é, –, and € correctly. Include it on every page.
  • <meta name="viewport" ...> tells mobile browsers to use the device width instead of zooming out. Include it on every page.
  • <title> sets the text in the browser tab. It is also used in bookmarks and search results.

items.title: <body>
items.text:
The <body> contains the content visitors see: headings, paragraphs, images, links, lists, tables, and forms.

<body>
  <h1>MHSM Bakery</h1>
  <p>Fresh bread is baked every morning.</p>
</body>

Each page has one <body>, and it comes after <head>.

The page structure: html wraps head and body

items.title: Check your work
items.text:
After you write a page, open it in a browser and look for these problems:

  • The page is blank. Check that the content is inside <body> and that you saved the file with an .html extension.
  • The tags appear as text. Check the file extension. A .txt file will not be rendered as a web page.
  • The text looks garbled. Check that <meta charset="utf-8"> is inside <head>.
  • The page is too wide on a phone. Check that the viewport meta tag is inside <head>.
  • Part of the page is missing. Check that each non-void element has a closing tag, and that tags do not cross each other.

items.title: Try it
items.text:
1. Create a folder called practice.
  2. Inside it, create a file called index.html.
  3. Type the page skeleton from this chapter, using your own title and two paragraphs about something you know well.
  4. Add a <strong> element around one important phrase.
  5. Open the file in your browser. If you change the file, save it and reload the browser.

Keep this file. The next chapters add to it.

Next: Headings shows how to outline a page.

items.title: Headings
items.text:
Headings divide a page into sections. They create the outline that readers, search engines, and screen readers use to understand the page.

HTML has six heading levels:

<h1>Page title</h1>
<h2>Main section</h2>
<h3>Subsection</h3>
<h4>Deeper subsection</h4>
<h5>Usually unnecessary</h5>
<h6>Usually unnecessary</h6>

Most pages only need <h1>, <h2>, and occasionally <h3>.

items.title: Start with one <h1>
items.text:
The <h1> is the main heading for the page. It should describe the whole page, not just the first paragraph.

<h1>MHSM Bakery</h1>
<p>Fresh bread and pastries, baked on site every morning.</p>

Use one <h1> per page. If you have two competing main topics, you probably need two pages.

items.title: Use <h2> for main sections
items.text:
An <h2> starts a major section under the page title:

<h1>MHSM Bakery</h1>

<h2>Bread</h2>
<p>White, brown, and whole wheat loaves are baked daily.</p>

<h2>Pastries</h2>
<p>Tea buns, doughnuts, and meat pies are available from 7am.</p>

The heading tells the reader what the section is about. The paragraph gives the detail.

items.title: Heading levels show hierarchy
items.text:
The number describes the level of the section, not the size of the text:

MHSM Bakery                  h1
├── Bread                    h2
│   ├── White bread          h3
│   └── Brown bread          h3
└── Pastries                 h2
    ├── Tea buns             h3
    └── Doughnuts            h3

Do not jump from <h1> to <h3> because you want smaller text. If a section belongs under an <h2>, use an <h3>. If it does not, keep it as an <h2>.

<!-- Avoid: the h3 skips a level -->
<h1>MHSM Bakery</h1>
<h3>Bread</h3>

<!-- Better -->
<h1>MHSM Bakery</h1>
<h2>Bread</h2>
<h3>White bread</h3>

You do not have to use every level. If there are no subsections, <h1> and <h2> are enough.

items.title: Headings are not for styling
items.text:
A common mistake is choosing <h3> because it looks smaller than <h2>. Heading levels describe structure. CSS controls size.

If you want normal text to look large, style the paragraph:

<p class="lead">Fresh bread is baked every morning.</p>

.lead {
  font-size: 1.25rem;
}

Changing the size of a heading does not change its level. A visually small <h1> is still the main heading.

items.title: Why this matters for accessibility
items.text:
Screen reader users can list all the headings on a page and jump between them. That only works when the headings form a sensible outline.

MHSM Bakery
  Bread
  Pastries
  Contact

Good headings also help sighted readers scan the page and help search engines understand which parts are important.

items.title: Check your work
items.text:
• Does the page have exactly one <h1>?
  • Does each <h2> introduce a real section?
  • Are there any skipped levels, such as <h1> followed directly by <h3>?
  • Would the page still make sense if you only read the headings?

items.title: Try it
items.text:
Open the page you started in the previous chapter. Add a short menu with:

  • one <h1> for the bakery name,
  • one <h2> for bread,
  • one <h2> for pastries,
  • one <h3> for a type of bread if you have more than one.

Reload the page. Then remove the text and read only the headings. They should still describe the page.

Next: Heading Levels is a quick reference and practice page for all six levels.

items.title: Heading Levels
items.text: This page is a quick reference for <h1> to <h6>. Use it when you need to check which level belongs where.

items.title: The six levels
items.text:
Tag Use Example <h1> Page title, once per page MHSM Bakery <h2> Major section Our Menu <h3> Subsection inside an <h2> Drinks <h4> Deeper subsection Hot Drinks <h5> Rarely needed Tea Notes <h6> Rarely needed Fine Print

The browser's default size is not a reason to choose a level. The outline is.

Default heading sizes, largest to smallest

items.title: A correct outline
items.text:
<h1>Bakery</h1>
  <h2>Menu</h2>
    <h3>Bread</h3>
    <h3>Pastries</h3>
  <h2>Prices</h2>
  <h2>Contact</h2>

This outline is valid even though it does not use <h4>, <h5>, or <h6>. Use only the levels your content needs.

items.title: An outline with a problem
items.text:
<h1>Bakery</h1>
  <h3>Menu</h3>
  <h3>Prices</h3>

The page jumps from level 1 to level 3. A screen reader user will hear a gap in the structure, and the page will be harder to scan.

items.title: Exercise: fix the outline
items.text:
The headings below are out of order. Rewrite them so they form a sensible outline with one <h1>, the main sections as <h2>, and the items under Bread as <h3>.

<h1>MHSM Bakery</h1>
<h3>Bread</h3>
<h4>White bread</h4>
<h4>Brown bread</h4>
<h3>Pastries</h3>
<h2>Contact</h2>

When you have rewritten it, check:

  • Is there exactly one <h1>?
  • Does every <h3> sit under an <h2>?
  • Does each heading describe the content below it?

items.title: Quick rules
items.text:
• One <h1> per page.
  • Do not skip levels.
  • Do not use headings just to make text bigger.
  • Keep heading text short and descriptive.
  • Use CSS to change appearance.

Next: Paragraphs

items.title: Paragraphs
items.text:
A paragraph is a block of text about one idea. HTML marks it with <p>:

<p>Fresh bread is baked every morning.</p>

Browsers put a paragraph on its own line and add space above and below it. Keep each paragraph short enough to read on a phone. If you start a new idea, start a new paragraph.

items.title: <p> and <br>
items.text:
<p> starts a new block. <br> breaks a line inside the same block.

<p>
  MHSM Bakery<br>
  Migadde, Uganda<br>
  Open 7am to 6pm
</p>

Use <br> for addresses, poems, song lyrics, or short lines that belong together. Do not use several <br> elements to create space between paragraphs:

<!-- Avoid -->
<p>Menu</p>
<br><br><br>
<p>Prices</p>

That creates no real spacing in the document structure, and screen readers do not treat the blank lines as meaningful. Use separate paragraphs and CSS margins instead.

Paragraphs create blocks; br creates a line break inside one block

items.title: <hr> marks a change of topic
items.text:
An <hr> is a thematic break. It separates sections when the topic changes, such as moving from a menu to prices or from one scene in a story to another.

<p>Our menu changes with the season.</p>
<hr>
<p>Prices include tax.</p>

The browser draws a line, but the line is not the point. The break in the content is.

Do not use <hr> as decoration. If you want a line for visual reasons, use a border in CSS.

items.title: Check your work
items.text:
• Does each paragraph contain one main idea?
  • Are there any groups of two or more <br> elements used for spacing?
  • Does <hr> separate two genuinely different topics?
  • Is all the text inside <p> or another suitable element, rather than loose in <body>?

items.title: Try it
items.text:
Mark up a shop notice with:

  • a heading,
  • two paragraphs about opening hours,
  • an address written with <br>,
  • an <hr> before a note about holiday closing times.

Open the page in the browser and resize the window. The line breaks in the address should stay; the paragraphs should wrap normally.

Next: Text Blocks gives the exact syntax for <p>, <br>, and <hr>.

items.title: Text Blocks
items.text: This is a syntax reference for the three block elements you will use most often.

items.title: <p>
items.text:
<p>Fresh bread is baked daily.</p>
  • Has an opening and closing tag.
  • Starts a new block.
  • Browsers add vertical space above and below it.
  • Do not put block elements such as another <p> or a <div> inside it.

items.title: <br>
items.text:
<p>
  MHSM Bakery<br>
  Migadde, Uganda<br>
  +256 700 000 000
</p>
  • Void element: no closing tag.
  • Breaks a line inside the current block.
  • Use it for addresses, poems, and short lines that belong together.
  • Do not use it to create margin or padding.

items.title: <hr>
items.text:
<p>Term one menu</p>
<hr>
<p>Term two menu</p>
  • Void element: no closing tag.
  • Represents a change of topic or scene.
  • The browser draws a line by default, but you can style it.
  • Do not use several <hr> elements in a row for decoration.

items.title: Reference
items.text: Element Closing tag Meaning Common mistake <p> Yes, </p> A block of text about one idea Using it for layout <br> No A line break inside a block Stacking several to fake spacing <hr> No A thematic break between sections Using it as a divider

items.title: Exercise: clean up the markup
items.text:
The page below uses the right tags in the wrong places. Rewrite it so the spacing comes from paragraphs, the address uses a line break, and the <hr> separates two topics.

<h1>MHSM Bakery</h1>

<p>We bake bread every morning.</p>
<br>
<br>
<br>

<p>Migadde, Uganda<br>Open 7am to 6pm</p>

<hr>

<hr>

<p>Holiday hours: 8am to noon.</p>

Check your version by opening it in the browser. There should be three clear ideas: the bakery, the contact details, and the holiday notice. The <hr> should appear once, between the contact details and the holiday notice.

Next: Build Your First Page

items.title: Build Your First Page
items.text: This chapter puts the previous lessons together. You will build a complete page with a title, sections, paragraphs, and a thematic break. The content is a school notice, but you can replace it with anything you know well.

items.title: 1. Create the file
items.text:
Create a folder for the exercise. Inside it, create a file called index.html.

Start with the page skeleton:

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>School Notice</title>
</head>
<body>

</body>
</html>

The <title> appears in the browser tab. The visible content goes inside <body>.

items.title: 2. Add the main heading
items.text:
<body>
  <h1>Sports Day</h1>
  <p>Sports Day will take place on Friday, 6 November.</p>
</body>

There is one <h1> because the page has one main topic.

items.title: 3. Add sections
items.text:
Use <h2> for the main parts of the notice:

<body>
  <h1>Sports Day</h1>
  <p>Sports Day will take place on Friday, 6 November.</p>

  <h2>Time and place</h2>
  <p>The event starts at 8am on the school field. Students should arrive by 7:30am.</p>

  <h2>What to bring</h2>
  <p>Bring a water bottle, a hat, and sports shoes. Lunch will be provided.</p>

  <h2>Parents and guardians</h2>
  <p>Parents are welcome to attend. Seating will be available near the finish line.</p>
</body>

Each <h2> introduces one section. Each paragraph gives the detail for that section.

items.title: 4. Add a closing note
items.text:
Use <hr> to separate the main notice from an unrelated note:

  <h2>Parents and guardians</h2>
  <p>Parents are welcome to attend. Seating will be available near the finish line.</p>

  <hr>

  <p>If it rains, the event will move to the school hall.</p>

Do not use several <br> elements to create the same gap.

items.title: 5. Check the page
items.text:
Open index.html in your browser. Check:

  • The browser tab shows "School Notice".
  • There is one main heading.
  • Every section has a heading and at least one paragraph.
  • The line under the closing note separates it from the main notice.
  • The page is readable when you make the browser window narrow.

items.title: 6. Improve the content
items.text:
Rewrite the notice for something you know: a football match, a school trip, a club meeting, or a shop opening. Keep the same structure:

  1. One <h1>.
  2. Two or three <h2> sections.
  3. One paragraph per idea.
  4. One <hr> only if you need a real break in topic.

items.title: What you have practised
items.text:
• Nesting elements inside <body>.
  • Choosing heading levels by structure, not size.
  • Writing paragraphs around one idea.
  • Using <hr> for a change of topic.
  • Checking a page in the browser instead of assuming it works.

Next: Emphasis and Meaning

items.title: Emphasis and Meaning
items.text:
HTML has several elements that make text stand out. Some describe meaning. Others only draw attention. Choosing the right one matters for screen readers, search engines, and anyone who later edits the page.

The rule: choose the element that describes the text, then use CSS if you need a different appearance.

items.title: <strong> for importance
items.text:
<strong> marks content that is important, serious, or urgent:

<p><strong>Warning:</strong> The exam starts at 8am.</p>

Browsers usually show it in bold, but the bold is not the point. The point is that the text carries more weight than the surrounding content.

<p>You <strong>must</strong> bring your student ID.</p>

If the text is not genuinely important, do not use <strong> just to make it bold.

items.title: <b> for attention without importance
items.text:
<b> draws attention without saying the text is more important:

<p>The <b>MHSM Bakery</b> stall is next to the library.</p>

It also renders bold by default. Use it when a word needs to stand out visually but does not carry extra meaning. Many pages do not need <b> at all; a class and CSS often make the intent clearer.

Element Meaning Default appearance <strong> This content is important Bold <b> Draw attention, no added importance Bold

items.title: <em> for emphasis
items.text:
<em> marks stress emphasis. It changes how a sentence should be read:

<p>You should <em>read the question</em> before answering.</p>

The stress falls on "read the question". Move the emphasis and the meaning changes:

<p><em>You</em> should read the question.</p>
<p>You should read <em>the question</em>.</p>

Browsers usually show emphasis in italics. Screen readers may also change the way they speak the word.

items.title: <i> for text set apart
items.text:
<i> marks text that is set apart by convention, without added emphasis:

<p>The scientific name for the mountain gorilla is <i>Gorilla beringei beringei</i>.</p>

<p>The French word <i>bonjour</i> means hello.</p>

Use <i> for titles of works only if the title is not already marked with <cite>, for foreign words, technical terms, and taxonomic names. Use <em> when you would stress the word in speech.

Element Meaning Default appearance <em> Stress emphasis Italic <i> Text set apart by convention Italic

items.title: <mark> for relevance
items.text:
<mark> highlights text that is relevant in the current context:

<p>Search results for <mark>bread</mark></p>
<p>The exam will cover <mark>HTML forms</mark> and tables.</p>

The highlight means "this matters here", not "this is important everywhere". Do not use <mark> for warnings. Use <strong> when the text itself is important.

items.title: Combining elements
items.text:
You can combine elements when both meanings apply:

<p><strong><em>Important:</em> Save your work before closing the editor.</strong></p>

Here <strong> marks the whole sentence as important, and <em> stresses the word "Important".

Do not stack elements to make text look more dramatic. If there is no meaning behind the markup, remove it.

items.title: Let CSS handle appearance
items.text:
You can keep the meaning and change the look:

<p><strong class="warning">Warning</strong></p>

.warning {
  color: #b00020;
  font-weight: normal;
}

The text is still important, even if it is not bold.

items.title: Quick reference
items.text: Question Element Is this important or urgent? <strong> Does it need vocal stress? <em> Should it draw the eye without added importance? <b> Is it a term, foreign word, or name set apart by convention? <i> Is it highlighted because it is relevant right now? <mark>

items.title: Exercise: choose the element
items.text:
Rewrite each sentence with the most suitable element. Be ready to explain your choice.

  1. Do not share your password with anyone.
  2. The word "sourdough" comes from the French word for sour.
  3. Your search matched 12 results for bread.
  4. The title of the book is Things Fall Apart.

One possible answer:

<p><strong>Do not share your password with anyone.</strong></p>
<p>The word <i>sourdough</i> comes from the French word for sour.</p>
<p>Your search matched <mark>12 results</mark> for bread.</p>
<p>The title of the book is <cite>Things Fall Apart</cite>.</p>

<cite> is covered in the next chapters. Use it for the title of a work.

Next: Code and Technical Text

items.title: Code and Technical Text
items.text: HTML has a small set of elements for text that is technical: code, keyboard input, program output, and variables. They are useful in tutorials, documentation, and any page that explains how something works.

items.title: Inline code with <code>
items.text:
Use <code> for a short piece of code inside a sentence:

<p>Use the <code>print()</code> function to display output.</p>

Browsers usually show it in a monospace font. The important part is that the markup says "this is code".

items.title: Code blocks with <pre> and <code>
items.text:
For more than one line, put <code> inside <pre>:

<pre><code>name = "Amina"
print(name)</code></pre>

<pre> preserves spaces and line breaks exactly as you type them. <code> says the content is code. Use both together for code blocks.

items.title: Showing HTML as text
items.text:
The browser treats HTML tags as markup. If you want to show a tag to the reader, escape the angle brackets:

<pre><code><p>Hello</p></code></pre>

That displays as:

<p>Hello</p>

Use < for < and > for >. You will need this whenever you write about HTML itself.

items.title: Keyboard input with <kbd>
items.text:
<kbd> marks a key or key combination:

<p>Press <kbd>Ctrl</kbd> + <kbd>S</kbd> to save the file.</p>

It is useful in instructions. Screen readers can identify it as keyboard input rather than ordinary text.

items.title: Program output with <samp>
items.text:
<samp> marks sample output from a program:

<p>The program returned:</p>
<p><samp>Hello, Amina</samp></p>

Use it when the text is something the computer produced.

items.title: Variables with <var>
items.text:
<var> marks a variable or placeholder in a mathematical expression or program:

<p>The area of a rectangle is <var>width</var> × <var>height</var>.</p>

items.title: Reference
items.text: Element Use Example <code> Inline code <code>print()</code> <pre> Preserve whitespace A code block or ASCII diagram <kbd> Keyboard input <kbd>Ctrl</kbd> <samp> Program output <samp>Build complete</samp> <var> Variable <var>total</var>

items.title: Exercise: mark up a recipe tool
items.text:
Create a small page that explains a command-line recipe tool. Include:

  • a sentence with inline code for the command name,
  • a code block with two commands,
  • a sentence describing a keyboard shortcut,
  • a sample output line,
  • one variable in a sentence about the recipe name.

Check that the code block keeps its indentation and that the angle brackets in any HTML example appear as text rather than disappearing.

Next: Small Semantic Tags

items.title: Small Semantic Tags
items.text: Some useful HTML elements do not change the page much. Their job is to add meaning that browsers and screen readers can use.

items.title: Abbreviations: <abbr>
items.text:
Use <abbr> for an abbreviation or acronym. The title attribute gives the full form:

<p>I am learning <abbr title="HyperText Markup Language">HTML</abbr>.</p>

The full form may appear as a tooltip when the reader hovers over the abbreviation. Do not use title to repeat information that is already visible.

items.title: Dates and times: <time>
items.text:
<time> marks a specific date, time, or duration:

<p>Sports Day starts at <time datetime="08:00">8am</time>.</p>
<p>The event is on <time datetime="2026-11-06">Friday, 6 November</time>.</p>

The text between the tags is for humans. The datetime attribute is machine-readable. It uses the format YYYY-MM-DD for dates and HH:MM for times.

You can also mark a duration:

<p>The journey takes <time datetime="PT2H30M">two and a half hours</time>.</p>

items.title: Deleted and inserted text: <del> and <ins>
items.text:
Use <del> for text that has been removed and <ins> for text that has been added:

<p>The price is <del>5,000</del> <ins>4,000</ins> shillings.</p>

Browsers usually show <del> with a line through it and <ins> underlined. This is useful for price changes, corrections, and showing edits. Add datetime if the time of the change matters.

items.title: Subscript and superscript
items.text:
<sub> lowers text below the baseline. <sup> raises it above the baseline.

<p>Water is H<sub>2</sub>O.</p>
<p>2<sup>3</sup> = 8.</p>

Do not use these elements just to move text around visually. Use CSS for positioning.

items.title: Reference
items.text: Element Meaning Example <abbr> Abbreviation or acronym <abbr title="World Health Organization">WHO</abbr> <time> Date, time, or duration <time datetime="2026-11-06">6 November</time> <del> Removed text <del>5,000</del> <ins> Inserted text <ins>4,000</ins> <sub> Subscript H<sub>2</sub>O <sup> Superscript 2<sup>3</sup>

items.title: Exercise: update a notice
items.text:
Take this notice and add the appropriate semantic tags:

<p>The WHO visit is on 6 November.</p>
<p>The meeting starts at 9am.</p>
<p>The old venue was the library. The new venue is the school hall.</p>
<p>The price of lunch is 5,000 shillings.</p>
<p>Water is H2O.</p>

Check that:

  • the abbreviation has a full form,
  • both dates and times use <time>,
  • the old and new information use <del> and <ins>,
  • the chemical formula uses <sub>.

Next: Quotations

items.title: Quotations
items.text: HTML has separate elements for a short quote inside a sentence and a longer quote set apart from the main text. It also has a way to name the source.

items.title: Short quotes: <q>
items.text:
Use <q> for a quotation inside a sentence:

<p>Our teacher said, <q>Read the question twice before you answer it.</q></p>

Browsers usually add quotation marks. Do not type the quotes yourself as well.

items.title: Block quotes: <blockquote>
items.text:
Use <blockquote> for a longer quotation that stands on its own:

<blockquote>
  <p>All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others.</p>
</blockquote>

A blockquote is a block element. Browsers usually indent it. If the quotation contains more than one paragraph, put each paragraph in its own <p> inside the blockquote.

items.title: Naming the source
items.text:
Use <cite> for the title of a work: a book, article, film, song, or report.

<blockquote>
  <p>All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others.</p>
</blockquote>
<p>George Orwell, <cite>Animal Farm</cite></p>

<cite> is not for the author's name. The author goes in ordinary text; the title goes in <cite>.

The cite attribute on <blockquote> can hold a URL for the source, but it is not visible on the page:

<blockquote cite="https://example.com/animal-farm">
  <p>All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others.</p>
</blockquote>

If readers need the source, add a visible link as well.

items.title: Reference
items.text: Element or attribute Use for <q> A short inline quotation <blockquote> A longer quotation set apart from the text <cite> The title of a work cite attribute A URL for the source of a quotation

items.title: Exercise: quote a book
items.text:
Find a sentence you like from a book, article, or speech. Add it to a page and include:

  • a <blockquote> for the quotation,
  • a visible source line,
  • <cite> around the title of the work,
  • a cite attribute if you have a URL for the source.

Check that the quotation marks appear once and that the source line names the work, not just the author.

Next: Address and Fine Print

items.title: Address and Fine Print
items.text: Two small elements often appear near the end of a page: <address> for contact information and <small> for secondary text.

items.title: <address>: contact information
items.text:
Use <address> for contact information for the author or owner of the page or section. It is not for any postal address that happens to appear in the content.

<address>
  MHSM Web Club<br>
  Makerere High School Migadde<br>
  <a href="mailto:webclub@example.com">webclub@example.com</a>
</address>

<address> is a block element. Browsers usually show it in italics. Contact information often belongs in a page footer:

<footer>
  <p>Questions? Contact the web club.</p>
  <address>
    <a href="mailto:webclub@example.com">webclub@example.com</a>
  </address>
</footer>

Do not use <address> for a shop's delivery address, a venue address, or a random location in the content. Use a normal paragraph for those.

items.title: <small>: fine print
items.text:
Use <small> for side comments, copyright notices, disclaimers, and attribution:

<p><small>Prices include tax and are valid until the end of the term.</small></p>

Browsers display it a little smaller than normal text. That does not make the content unimportant. It means the content is secondary:

<footer>
  <p><small>© 2026 MHSM Web Club. All rights reserved.</small></p>
</footer>

Do not use <small> to hide important information, and do not use it just because you want smaller text. Use CSS for styling.

items.title: Reference
items.text: Element Use for Avoid <address> Contact details for the page or section author Any postal address in the content <small> Copyright, disclaimers, attribution Hiding important information

items.title: Exercise: add a footer
items.text:
Add a footer to a page you have already built. Include:

  • one sentence about who made the page,
  • an <address> with an email link,
  • a <small> copyright line with the current year.

Check that the email link uses mailto: and that the address is contact information, not a location mentioned in the page content.

Next: Links

items.title: Links
items.text:
Links let readers move between pages, jump to a section, or send an email. HTML uses the anchor element, <a>, for all of these.

<a href="menu.html">See the menu</a>
  • <a> creates the link.
  • href says where the link goes.
  • The text between the tags is what readers click.

items.title: Linking to another website
items.text:
Use the full URL, including https://:

<p>Visit the <a href="https://www.python.org">Python website</a>.</p>

This is an absolute URL because it contains the full address.

items.title: Linking to your own pages
items.text:
Use a relative path when the target is part of your site:

website/
├── index.html
├── menu.html
└── contact.html

<a href="menu.html">Menu</a>
<a href="contact.html">Contact</a>

If the file is inside a folder, include the folder name:

website/
├── index.html
└── pages/
    ├── menu.html
    └── contact.html

<a href="pages/menu.html">Menu</a>

The path is relative to the page containing the link. A broken link is usually a filename or folder mistake.

items.title: Opening a link in a new tab
items.text:
Add target="_blank" to open the link in a new tab:

<a href="https://www.python.org" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Python</a>

Only do this for links where leaving the page would interrupt the reader. Avoid opening every link in a new tab. When you use target="_blank", add rel="noopener" so the new page cannot control the original tab through window.opener.

items.title: Linking to an email address
items.text:
Use mailto::

<a href="mailto:webclub@example.com">Email the web club</a>

The browser will try to open the reader's email application.

items.title: Linking to a section on the same page
items.text:
Give the target element an id, then link to it with #:

<h2 id="contact">Contact</h2>

<p><a href="#contact">Go to contact details</a></p>

The id must be unique on the page. The link scrolls to the element with that id.

items.title: Linking an image
items.text:
An image can be the clickable content:

<a href="menu.html">
  <img src="images/bread.jpg" alt="See the bread menu" width="300">
</a>

If the image is the only content of the link, its alt text should describe the link destination.

items.title: Navigation
items.text:
A group of links can become site navigation:

<nav>
  <a href="index.html">Home</a>
  <a href="menu.html">Menu</a>
  <a href="contact.html">Contact</a>
</nav>

<nav> is covered in the page landmarks chapter. For now, remember that navigation is still a group of links.

items.title: Complete example
items.text:
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>MHSM Bakery</title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>MHSM Bakery</h1>

  <nav>
    <a href="index.html">Home</a>
    <a href="menu.html">Menu</a>
    <a href="contact.html">Contact</a>
  </nav>

  <p>
    Read about our bread on the <a href="menu.html">menu page</a>.
  </p>

  <p>
    You can also visit the
    <a href="https://www.python.org" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Python website</a>.
  </p>
</body>
</html>

items.title: Check your work
items.text:
• Click every link. It should go to the page or section you expected.
  • Check the spelling and capitalisation of file names. Menu.html and menu.html are different on many servers.
  • Do not use "click here" as link text. Describe the destination instead.
  • Add rel="noopener" when you use target="_blank".

items.title: Try it
items.text:
Create two pages, index.html and contact.html, in the same folder. On index.html:

  1. Add a <nav> with a link to contact.html.
  2. Add a link to an external website.
  3. Add a section with id="hours" and a link that jumps to it.
  4. Add a mailto: link.

Open the page and test each link. Then rename contact.html to contact-us.html without updating the link and see what the browser reports. Fix the link afterwards.

Next: Images

items.title: Images
items.text:
Images can explain something faster than text, but they also need care. An image without useful alt text is invisible to screen reader users, and an image without dimensions can make the page jump while it loads.

The element is <img>:

<img src="bread.jpg" alt="A loaf of brown bread on a wooden table">

<img> is a void element, so it has no closing tag. It has two required attributes in practice: src and alt.

items.title: src: where the image is
items.text:
src is the path to the image file:

<img src="bread.jpg" alt="A loaf of brown bread">

If the image is in a folder:

<img src="images/bread.jpg" alt="A loaf of brown bread">

You can also use a full URL:

<img src="https://example.com/bread.jpg" alt="A loaf of brown bread">

For your own projects, keep images in a folder such as images/ and use relative paths.

items.title: alt: a text description
items.text:
alt describes the image for people who cannot see it. It is used by screen readers, shown when the image fails to load, and read by search engines.

<img src="gorilla.jpg" alt="A mountain gorilla sitting in tall grass">

Write what matters about the image in context, not a list of every detail. Ask: if this image were removed, what would the reader miss?

items.title: Images that are only decoration
items.text:
If an image is purely decorative and the surrounding text already explains everything, use an empty alt:

<img src="divider.png" alt="">

Do not write alt="image" or alt="picture of...". Those words add no information.

items.title: Images inside links
items.text:
If an image is the only content of a link, the alt text should describe the destination:

<a href="menu.html">
  <img src="menu-icon.png" alt="See the menu" width="40" height="40">
</a>

items.title: Width and height
items.text:
The width and height attributes give the browser the image's dimensions:

<img
  src="bread.jpg"
  alt="A loaf of brown bread"
  width="400"
  height="300"
>

Providing both helps the browser reserve space before the image loads, which prevents the page from shifting. CSS can change the displayed size later.

items.title: Figures and captions
items.text:
Use <figure> and <figcaption> when an image needs a visible caption:

<figure>
  <img
    src="gorilla.jpg"
    alt="A mountain gorilla sitting in tall grass"
    width="500"
    height="350"
  >
  <figcaption>A mountain gorilla in Mgahinga Gorilla National Park.</figcaption>
</figure>
  • <figure> groups the image with its caption.
  • <figcaption> holds the visible caption.

Alt text and captions do different jobs. Alt text is for people who cannot see the image. The caption is visible to everyone and adds context.

items.title: Check your work
items.text:
• Does every <img> have src and alt?
  • Is the alt text a useful description, not a filename?
  • Are purely decorative images marked with alt=""?
  • Does the image path match the actual file name and folder?
  • Do images have width and height so the page does not jump?
  • Does the image still make sense at a narrow window width?

items.title: Try it
items.text:
Add an image to a page you have already built. Include:

  1. a relative path to an image in an images/ folder,
  2. useful alt text,
  3. width and height,
  4. a <figure> and <figcaption> if the image needs a visible caption.

Then temporarily change the file name in src and reload. Read the alt text in the broken image. Would someone who cannot see the picture still understand what was there? Fix the path afterwards.

Next: Lists

items.title: Lists
items.text: Lists group related items and keep the relationship between them clear. HTML has three main list types.

items.title: Unordered lists: <ul>
items.text:
Use <ul> when the order of the items does not matter:

<ul>
  <li>Bread</li>
  <li>Milk</li>
  <li>Eggs</li>
</ul>

Browsers show each item with a bullet. Every item goes inside <li>.

items.title: Ordered lists: <ol>
items.text:
Use <ol> when the order matters:

<ol>
  <li>Mix the flour and water.</li>
  <li>Knead the dough for ten minutes.</li>
  <li>Bake at 220°C.</li>
</ol>

Browsers number the items automatically. You can change the starting number:

<ol start="5">
  <li>Fifth step</li>
  <li>Sixth step</li>
</ol>

items.title: Nested lists
items.text:
A nested list goes inside an <li>, not after it:

<ul>
  <li>
    Bread
    <ul>
      <li>White</li>
      <li>Brown</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
  <li>Milk</li>
</ul>

This creates a sub-list under "Bread". The outer list still has two items.

items.title: Description lists: <dl>
items.text:
Use <dl> for term and definition pairs:

<dl>
  <dt>HTML</dt>
  <dd>The structure and meaning of a page.</dd>

  <dt>CSS</dt>
  <dd>The presentation of a page.</dd>
</dl>
  • <dl> is the list.
  • <dt> is the term.
  • <dd> is the definition.

Description lists are useful for glossaries, menus with descriptions, and metadata.

items.title: Rules for list markup
items.text:
• Only <li> may be a direct child of <ul> or <ol>.
  • Keep the entire nested list inside the <li> it belongs to.
  • Do not fake a list with dashes or <br>. You lose the structure and screen readers cannot announce the number of items.
  • Navigation menus are often lists. You will see <nav><ul>...</ul></nav> in real pages.

items.title: Exercise: build a shop list
items.text:
Create a page with:

  1. An unordered list of three bread types.
  2. A nested list under one bread type showing two sizes.
  3. An ordered list of four steps for making tea.
  4. A description list with two terms and their definitions.

Check that each nested list is inside an <li> and that every item uses <li>. Then use the browser's accessibility inspector, if available, to confirm the list is announced as a list.

Next: Tables

items.title: Tables
items.text: Tables are for data that belongs in rows and columns: marks, prices, timetables, and records. They are not for page layout. CSS handles layout now.

items.title: The basic structure
items.text:
A table contains rows, and each row contains cells:

<table>
  <tr>
    <td>John</td>
    <td>15</td>
    <td>S2</td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td>Sarah</td>
    <td>14</td>
    <td>S1</td>
  </tr>
</table>
  • <table> creates the table.
  • <tr> creates a row.
  • <td> creates a data cell.

The example above is hard to read because the first row is data, not headings. Tables usually need header cells.

items.title: Header cells: <th>
items.text:
Use <th> for header cells. Add scope="col" for column headings and scope="row" for row headings:

<table>
  <tr>
    <th scope="col">Name</th>
    <th scope="col">Age</th>
    <th scope="col">Class</th>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td>John</td>
    <td>15</td>
    <td>S2</td>
  </tr>
</table>

scope tells assistive technology which cells a heading applies to. It is especially important in larger tables.

items.title: A caption
items.text:
Give the table a title with <caption>:

<table>
  <caption>Student Information</caption>
  <tr>
    <th scope="col">Name</th>
    <th scope="col">Age</th>
    <th scope="col">Class</th>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td>John</td>
    <td>15</td>
    <td>S2</td>
  </tr>
</table>

The caption goes immediately after <table>. It helps everyone understand what the table contains.

items.title: Grouping rows
items.text:
Longer tables can be grouped into a head, body, and foot:

<table>
  <caption>Bakery Prices</caption>

  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th scope="col">Item</th>
      <th scope="col">Price</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>

  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <td>Bread</td>
      <td>5,000</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Milk</td>
      <td>3,000</td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>

  <tfoot>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Total</th>
      <td>8,000</td>
    </tr>
  </tfoot>
</table>
  • <thead> groups the header rows.
  • <tbody> groups the main data rows.
  • <tfoot> groups summary or footer rows.

Grouping is useful for styling and for very long tables. A small table does not always need all three.

items.title: Spanning cells
items.text:
Use colspan when a cell should cover more than one column:

<tr>
  <th scope="colgroup" colspan="2">Student Information</th>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td>John</td>
  <td>S2</td>
</tr>

Use rowspan when a cell should cover more than one row:

<tr>
  <th scope="rowgroup" rowspan="2">Name</th>
  <td>John</td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td>Sarah</td>
</tr>

Spanning makes a table harder to read and harder to maintain. Use it only when the data really has that shape.

items.title: A complete timetable
items.text:
<table>
  <caption>Term Two Timetable</caption>

  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th scope="col">Time</th>
      <th scope="col">Monday</th>
      <th scope="col">Tuesday</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>

  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">8:00</th>
      <td>Mathematics</td>
      <td>English</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">9:00</th>
      <td>Biology</td>
      <td>Chemistry</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">10:00</th>
      <td colspan="2">Break</td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

The row headings make it clear which time each row describes. The break spans both days.

items.title: Check your work
items.text:
• Is the table used for data, not layout?
  • Does it have a caption?
  • Are column headings <th scope="col"> and row headings <th scope="row">?
  • Does every row have the right number of cells?
  • Does the table still make sense when read aloud row by row?

items.title: Try it
items.text:
Build a table for a class timetable or a price list. Include:

  1. a caption,
  2. column headings with scope="col",
  3. at least three rows of data,
  4. one row heading with scope="row",
  5. one cell that spans two columns, only if the data needs it.

Open the page and check that the columns line up. Then add a long item name and see whether the table stays readable.

Next: Forms

items.title: Forms
items.text:
Forms collect information from the reader: a login, a search, a registration, or a message. A form is a set of controls inside a <form> element.

<form>
  <p>
    <label for="name">Name</label>
    <input type="text" id="name" name="name">
  </p>
  <button type="submit">Submit</button>
</form>

The form above has a label, a text field, and a submit button. It does not send the data anywhere yet because the action is missing.

items.title: Labels
items.text:
Every input needs a label. Use <label for="..."> and match it to the input's id:

<label for="email">Email</label>
<input type="email" id="email" name="email">

The for value must match the id exactly. Clicking the label then focuses the input, and screen readers can announce which field is which.

Do not replace a label with a placeholder. Placeholders disappear as soon as the reader types.

items.title: Input types
items.text:
The type attribute changes what the input accepts and which keyboard appears on mobile:

Type Use for text General single-line text email Email addresses password Passwords, hidden as typed number Numbers date A date time A time search Search terms checkbox Several choices radio One choice from a group file Uploading a file submit A submit button 
<label for="age">Age</label>
<input type="number" id="age" name="age" min="10" max="100">

Browsers can validate some types. An email input rejects text that does not look like an email address, and required blocks an empty submission.

items.title: Longer text: <textarea>
items.text:
Use <textarea> for multiple lines:

<label for="message">Message</label>
<textarea id="message" name="message" rows="5"></textarea>

The rows attribute sets the visible height. It is a starting size, not a character limit.

items.title: Drop-down lists: <select> and <option>
items.text:
<label for="country">Country</label>
<select id="country" name="country">
  <option value="uganda">Uganda</option>
  <option value="kenya">Kenya</option>
  <option value="tanzania">Tanzania</option>
</select>

Each <option> is one choice. The value is what gets submitted.

items.title: Radio buttons: one choice
items.text:
Radio buttons in the same group share a name. Only one can be selected.

<fieldset>
  <legend>Year of study</legend>

  <label>
    <input type="radio" name="year" value="s1">
    S1
  </label>

  <label>
    <input type="radio" name="year" value="s2">
    S2
  </label>
</fieldset>

<fieldset> groups related controls. <legend> gives the group a name. This is much clearer than putting the question in a separate paragraph.

items.title: Checkboxes: several choices
items.text:
Checkboxes use the same name when they belong to one question, but each can be selected independently:

<fieldset>
  <legend>Languages you know</legend>

  <label>
    <input type="checkbox" name="language" value="python">
    Python
  </label>

  <label>
    <input type="checkbox" name="language" value="javascript">
    JavaScript
  </label>
</fieldset>

items.title: name and value
items.text:
• id identifies the element within the page. It connects a label to its control.
  • name identifies the field when the form is submitted.
  • value is the data sent for that control.
<label for="username">Username</label>
<input type="text" id="username" name="username">

If a field has no name, its value is not submitted.

items.title: Required fields and placeholders
items.text:
<label for="email">Email</label>
<input
  type="email"
  id="email"
  name="email"
  placeholder="you@example.com"
  required
>

required makes the field mandatory. placeholder shows a temporary hint inside the field. Use a placeholder for an example format, not as a replacement for a label.

items.title: Submitting the form
items.text:
A submit button sends the form:

<button type="submit">Register</button>

Use type="button" for a button that should not submit the form.

The action attribute says where the data goes, and method says how:

<form action="/register" method="post">
  • GET puts the values in the URL. It is suitable for searches and requests that do not change data.
  • POST sends the values in the request body. It is suitable for registrations, logins, and other changes.

You will need a server to process the data. For now, focus on the markup and the browser's built-in validation.

items.title: A complete registration form
items.text:
<form action="/register" method="post">
  <h2>Create an account</h2>

  <p>
    <label for="name">Name</label>
    <input type="text" id="name" name="name" required>
  </p>

  <p>
    <label for="email">Email</label>
    <input type="email" id="email" name="email" required>
  </p>

  <p>
    <label for="password">Password</label>
    <input type="password" id="password" name="password" required>
  </p>

  <fieldset>
    <legend>Year of study</legend>
    <label>
      <input type="radio" name="year" value="s1">
      S1
    </label>
    <label>
      <input type="radio" name="year" value="s2">
      S2
    </label>
  </fieldset>

  <p>
    <label for="country">Country</label>
    <select id="country" name="country">
      <option value="uganda">Uganda</option>
      <option value="kenya">Kenya</option>
      <option value="tanzania">Tanzania</option>
    </select>
  </p>

  <p>
    <label for="message">About you</label>
    <textarea id="message" name="message" rows="4"></textarea>
  </p>

  <button type="submit">Register</button>
</form>

The fields are wrapped in paragraphs so they appear on separate lines. CSS can arrange them in columns later.

items.title: Check your work
items.text:
• Does every input have a label?
  • Does every label's for match an input id?
  • Do radio buttons in one group share a name?
  • Are radio buttons and checkboxes inside a <fieldset> with a <legend>?
  • Does every control that should be submitted have a name?
  • Did you use required only on fields that are genuinely required?
  • Does the form still make sense when navigated with the Tab key?

items.title: Try it
items.text:
Build a contact form with:

  1. a name field,
  2. an email field,
  3. a drop-down for the reason for contact,
  4. a radio group for preferred contact method,
  5. a message textarea,
  6. a submit button.

Open the form and try to submit it while the required fields are empty. Read the browser's message. Then fill it in and check that the fields accept the expected input.

Next: Grouping Content

items.title: Grouping Content
items.text: As a page grows, you need to group related content. HTML has two block containers, <div> and <section>, and one inline container, <span>. They look similar in the browser but mean different things.

items.title: <div>: a generic block
items.text:
<div> groups content without saying what the group is:

<div>
  <h2>About us</h2>
  <p>We teach students how to build websites.</p>
</div>

Use <div> when no more specific element describes the group. It is common for layout and for CSS or JavaScript hooks.

A <div> can contain headings, paragraphs, links, and other blocks:

<div class="contact">
  <h2>Contact</h2>
  <p>Email: <a href="mailto:webclub@example.com">webclub@example.com</a></p>
</div>

items.title: <section>: a thematic section
items.text:
<section> groups content that forms a distinct part of the document:

<section>
  <h2>Our courses</h2>
  <p>We teach HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.</p>
</section>

The difference from <div> is meaning. A <section> says "this is a section of the page", not just "these elements are grouped".

A section usually has a heading. Without a heading, it is hard for readers and assistive technology to know what the section is for. If the group has no heading and no semantic meaning, use a <div>.

items.title: <span>: a generic inline container
items.text:
<span> groups a small piece of content inside a line:

<p>My favourite language is <span class="highlight">Python</span>.</p>

<span> does not start a new line. Use it when you need to style or target part of a sentence. Without a class, id, or script, a <span> does nothing.

items.title: Choosing between them
items.text:
Element Display Meaning Use when <section> Block A distinct thematic section The content has its own heading and topic <div> Block No semantic meaning You need a generic block for layout or styling <span> Inline No semantic meaning You need to target part of a line

If the content is a page header, navigation, main content, article, sidebar, or footer, use the semantic landmarks from the next chapter instead of a <div>.

items.title: Classes and ids
items.text:
Grouping elements become more useful with class and id.

A class can be shared by several elements:

<section class="course">
  <h2>HTML</h2>
</section>

<section class="course">
  <h2>CSS</h2>
</section>

An id identifies one element:

<div id="main-content">
  <h1>Welcome</h1>
</div>

Use classes for styling groups and ids for in-page links or JavaScript hooks. Do not use the same id twice on a page.

items.title: A complete example
items.text:
<section>
  <h2>Our courses</h2>

  <div class="course">
    <h3>HTML</h3>
    <p>Learn how to structure a <span class="term">web page</span>.</p>
  </div>

  <div class="course">
    <h3>CSS</h3>
    <p>Learn how to style the <span class="term">same page</span>.</p>
  </div>
</section>
  • <section> groups the courses section.
  • Each <div> groups one course.
  • Each <span> marks a phrase inside a paragraph.

The <div> elements could be <article> elements because each course is a self-contained item. The next chapter explains when that is a better choice.

items.title: Exercise: choose the wrapper
items.text:
For each item, choose <section>, <div>, or <span> and explain why:

  1. A group of three news stories, each with its own heading.
  2. A wrapper that only exists to apply a grid layout.
  3. The word "sold out" inside a product paragraph.
  4. A "Contact us" block with a heading and two paragraphs.

Check your answers against these questions:

  • Does the group have its own heading and topic?
  • Is the group only needed for layout or styling?
  • Is the content inline or block-level?

Next: Page Landmarks

items.title: Page Landmarks
items.text: HTML has elements that describe the purpose of each part of a page. They help screen readers, search engines, and anyone reading your code.

items.title: A typical page
items.text:
<body>
  <header>
    <h1>MHSM Web Club</h1>
  </header>

  <nav>
    <a href="index.html">Home</a>
    <a href="projects.html">Projects</a>
    <a href="contact.html">Contact</a>
  </nav>

  <main>
    <article>
      <h2>Our first project</h2>
      <p>The club built a page for the school library.</p>
    </article>

    <aside>
      <h2>Related</h2>
      <p>Read about the CSS track next.</p>
    </aside>
  </main>

  <footer>
    <p>© 2026 MHSM Web Club</p>
  </footer>
</body>

Each element tells the browser something about its content. The layout is still controlled by CSS.

items.title: <header>
items.text:
<header> holds introductory content for a page or section: a title, logo, or short introduction.

<header>
  <h1>MHSM Web Club</h1>
  <p>Student projects from Makerere High School Migadde.</p>
</header>

A header can also belong to an article:

<article>
  <header>
    <h2>Our first project</h2>
    <p>Published 1 October 2026</p>
  </header>
  <p>The club built a page for the school library.</p>
</article>

The inner header belongs to the article, not the whole page.

items.title: <nav>
items.text:
<nav> wraps major navigation links:

<nav>
  <a href="index.html">Home</a>
  <a href="projects.html">Projects</a>
  <a href="contact.html">Contact</a>
</nav>

Use it for the main site navigation, a table of contents, or another important group of links. Do not wrap every link in <nav>. A link inside a paragraph is just a link.

items.title: <main>
items.text:
<main> holds the primary content of the page:

<main>
  <h1>About the club</h1>
  <p>The club meets every Wednesday after school.</p>
</main>

Use one <main> per page. Do not put the site navigation, header, or footer inside it.

items.title: <footer>
items.text:
<footer> holds information about the page or section: copyright, contact details, or related links.

<footer>
  <p>© 2026 MHSM Web Club</p>
  <a href="contact.html">Contact us</a>
</footer>

Like <header>, it can belong to the page or to an article.

items.title: <article>
items.text:
<article> is for a self-contained piece of content that would still make sense on its own:

  • a blog post,
  • a news story,
  • a forum post,
  • a product review.
<article>
  <h2>Library page launched</h2>
  <p>The new page lists opening hours and available books.</p>
</article>

A page can contain several articles:

<main>
  <h1>Club news</h1>

  <article>
    <h2>Library page launched</h2>
    <p>The new page lists opening hours and available books.</p>
  </article>

  <article>
    <h2>New members welcome</h2>
    <p>The club meets every Wednesday after school.</p>
  </article>
</main>

items.title: <aside>
items.text:
<aside> is for content related to the main content but not part of it: a sidebar, related links, or a short note.

<aside>
  <h2>Related</h2>
  <p>Read the CSS track to learn how to style this page.</p>
</aside>

Inside an article, an aside might hold a definition or a related fact. If the content is essential to understanding the page, it belongs in the main content instead.

items.title: Section or article?
items.text:
• <section> groups content by topic. It is a part of the page.
  • <article> is a self-contained piece that could be published on its own.
<main>
  <section>
    <h2>Latest articles</h2>

    <article>
      <h3>Library page launched</h3>
      <p>The new page lists opening hours and available books.</p>
    </article>

    <article>
      <h3>New members welcome</h3>
      <p>The club meets every Wednesday after school.</p>
    </article>
  </section>
</main>

The section groups the latest articles. Each article is an independent piece inside that group.

items.title: Semantic HTML compared with div soup
items.text:
You could build the same page with only <div> elements:

<div>
  <div>
    <h1>MHSM Web Club</h1>
  </div>
  <div>
    <a href="index.html">Home</a>
    <a href="projects.html">Projects</a>
  </div>
  <div>
    <h2>Library page launched</h2>
    <p>The new page lists opening hours.</p>
  </div>
</div>

It renders, but it does not say what each part is. Compare:

<header>
  <h1>MHSM Web Club</h1>
</header>

The second version tells the browser and screen reader that this is the page header.

items.title: Exercise: convert a div-only page
items.text:
Rewrite this page using <header>, <nav>, <main>, <article>, <aside>, and <footer>:

<div>
  <div>
    <h1>MHSM Web Club</h1>
  </div>

  <div>
    <a href="index.html">Home</a>
    <a href="projects.html">Projects</a>
  </div>

  <div>
    <h2>Library page launched</h2>
    <p>The new page lists opening hours and available books.</p>
  </div>

  <div>
    <p>© 2026 MHSM Web Club</p>
  </div>
</div>

Check that:

  • there is one <main>,
  • the navigation is inside <nav>,
  • the article has its own heading,
  • the copyright line is inside <footer>,
  • no <div> remains unless it is needed for layout.

items.title: Reference
items.text:
Element Purpose <header> Introductory content for a page or section <nav> Major navigation links <main> Primary content of the page <article> Self-contained content <aside> Related but secondary content <footer> Footer information for a page or section

Next: continue with the CSS course.

items.title: CSS Course
items.text:
HTML gives a page structure and meaning. CSS controls how that structure looks: colour, type, spacing, and layout.

This track follows the HTML course. You will use the same index.html file and add a separate stylesheet.

Start with What is CSS?

items.title: Before you start
items.text:
You should be able to build a simple HTML page with headings, paragraphs, links, and images. If not, work through the HTML course first.

You need a folder containing an HTML file and a CSS file. Keep them in the same folder so the path is easy to manage.

items.title: Linking a stylesheet
items.text:
Add this line inside <head>:

<link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">

The href must match the CSS file name exactly. If the file is in a folder, include the folder in the path:

<link rel="stylesheet" href="css/styles.css">

If the styles do not appear, check the file name and path first. That is the most common mistake.

items.title: How to use this track
items.text:
• Type the examples instead of copying them.
  • Change one value at a time and reload the browser.
  • Use the browser's developer tools to inspect the element and see which CSS rules apply.
  • Keep a small project open while you read. The practice chapters make more sense when you have a page to style.

items.title: Chapters
items.text: The chapter numbers are the recommended order. The groups below match that order.

items.title: Foundations
items.text:
• What is CSS?: rules, declarations, and where to put CSS.
  • Box Model: content, padding, border, margin, and box-sizing.
  • Selectors: type, class, id, attribute, and combinators.
  • Nesting: write related selectors inside one rule.

items.title: How CSS is applied
items.text:
• The Cascade: source order, origins, and importance.
  • Specificity: which selector wins.
  • Inheritance: which properties flow from parent to child.

items.title: Values and colour
items.text:
• Color: hex, rgb, hsl, and currentColor.
  • Sizing: px, rem, em, percentages, and viewport units.

items.title: Layout
items.text:
• Layout: normal flow and positioning.
  • Flexbox: one-dimensional layout.
  • Grid: two-dimensional layout.
  • Logical Properties: inline and block instead of left and right.

items.title: Reusable values and spacing
items.text:
• Custom Properties: reusable values with var().
  • Spacing: padding, margin, gap, and a spacing scale.

items.title: Appearance
items.text:
• Pseudo-elements: ::before, ::after, and text fragments.
  • Pseudo-classes: :hover, :focus-visible, and structural states.
  • Borders: width, style, colour, and radius.
  • Shadows: box-shadow and text-shadow.

items.title: Typography and responsive design
items.text:
• Typography: fonts, sizes, and readable text.
  • Responsive: fluid layouts and media queries.

items.title: Finishing
items.text:
• Functions: calc(), min(), max(), and clamp().
  • Practice: Build a Page: put the whole track together.

items.title: What you should be able to do at the end
items.text:
• Link a stylesheet and explain why a rule is not applying.
  • Use classes and a small set of reusable values.
  • Build a page layout with flexbox or grid.
  • Make text readable and colour contrast accessible.
  • Adjust a page for narrow screens without duplicating all your CSS.

CSS describes presentation. HTML still describes meaning. Keep that split and both languages stay simpler.

items.title: What is CSS?
items.text: CSS controls how HTML looks. A paragraph is still a paragraph, but CSS decides its colour, size, spacing, and position on the page.

items.title: A first rule
items.text:
p {
  color: #333;
  line-height: 1.6;
}

A rule has a selector and a declaration block:

p          selector: which elements to style
{ }        declaration block
color      property
#333       value

Read it as: select every <p> element, then apply these declarations.

A rule can have several declarations:

h1 {
  font-size: 2rem;
  margin-bottom: 0.5rem;
}

items.title: External stylesheet
items.text:
Put CSS in a separate file and link it from <head>:

<head>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">
</head>

/* styles.css */
body {
  font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
}

This is the normal choice. It keeps HTML readable and lets you reuse the same styles on several pages.

items.title: Internal stylesheet
items.text:
A <style> block inside <head> works for small tests:

<style>
  p {
    color: crimson;
  }
</style>

Use it for quick experiments, not for a whole site.

items.title: Inline styles
items.text:
An inline style applies to one element:

<p style="color: crimson;">Hello</p>

Avoid inline styles for normal styling. They are hard to reuse and hard to override.

items.title: A starting stylesheet
items.text:
Start a project with a small reset and readable defaults:

* {
  box-sizing: border-box;
}

body {
  margin: 0;
  font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
  line-height: 1.6;
  color: #222;
}

box-sizing: border-box makes width calculations easier. The body rule sets a readable font and removes the browser's default margin.

items.title: Check your work
items.text:
If your styles do not apply:

  • Check the stylesheet path in href.
  • Check that the CSS file is saved with a .css extension.
  • Check that the <link> is inside <head>.
  • Check for a missing } or ; in the CSS file.
  • Reload the page after saving.

items.title: Try it
items.text:
1. Create index.html and styles.css in the same folder.
  2. Link the stylesheet from the HTML file.
  3. Add a heading and two paragraphs.
  4. Change the body font, text colour, and line height in the CSS.
  5. Add a rule that makes all links a different colour.

If nothing changes, fix the link before adding more CSS.

Next: Box Model

items.title: Box Model
items.text:
Every element is a rectangular box. The box has four layers, from inside out:

margin
┌─────────────────────────┐
│ border                  │
│ ┌─────────────────────┐ │
│ │ padding             │ │
│ │ ┌─────────────────┐ │ │
│ │ │ content         │ │ │
│ │ └─────────────────┘ │ │
│ └─────────────────────┘ │
└─────────────────────────┘
  • Content: the text or image.
  • Padding: space inside the border, around the content.
  • Border: the edge of the box.
  • Margin: space outside the border, between this box and its neighbours.

items.title: Seeing the box model
items.text:
<div class="card">Hello</div>

.card {
  width: 240px;
  padding: 16px;
  border: 2px solid #333;
  margin: 24px;
}

By default, width sets the content width only. The visible box is wider because padding and border are added:

visible width = width + padding left + padding right + border left + border right

That default is called content-box and it catches almost everyone at least once.

items.title: box-sizing
items.text:
Set box-sizing: border-box once at the top of the stylesheet:

* {
  box-sizing: border-box;
}

.card {
  width: 240px;
  padding: 16px;
  border: 2px solid #333;
}

Now 240px includes the padding and border. This makes widths easier to reason about, especially in layouts.

items.title: Padding and margin
items.text:
• Padding is inside the box. The background colour covers it.
  • Margin is outside the box. The background does not cover it.
.card {
  padding: 1rem;
}

.card + .card {
  margin-top: 1rem;
}

Use padding when you want more space around the content inside a box. Use margin when you want space between boxes.

items.title: Shorthand
items.text:
/* all four sides */
margin: 1rem;

/* vertical | horizontal */
padding: 0.5rem 1rem;

/* top | horizontal | bottom */
margin: 1rem 0 2rem;

/* top | right | bottom | left */
padding: 1rem 1.5rem 1rem 1.5rem;

The same pattern works for border, although you also need a width, style, and colour:

.card {
  border: 1px solid #ddd;
}

items.title: Margin collapse
items.text:
Vertical margins between block elements can collapse. The larger margin wins:

h2 {
  margin-bottom: 1rem;
}

p {
  margin-top: 1rem;
}

The gap between them is 1rem, not 2rem. This is normal. If you need exact spacing, use padding or gap in a flex or grid container.

items.title: Try it
items.text:
1. Add a card to a page with a background colour, padding, border, and margin.
  2. Open the browser's developer tools and inspect the card.
  3. Find the box model diagram in the styles panel. Hover over the content, padding, border, and margin areas to see them highlighted.
  4. Change box-sizing from border-box to content-box and compare the visible width.
  5. Put the setting back.

If the box is wider than you expected, check whether box-sizing is set.

Next: Selectors

items.title: Selectors
items.text: A selector tells the browser which elements a rule applies to. Good selectors keep CSS small and predictable.

items.title: Type selectors
items.text:
A type selector targets an element name:

p {
  color: #333;
}

h2 {
  margin-top: 2rem;
}

Use type selectors for base styles that should apply everywhere.

items.title: Class selectors
items.text:
A class selector targets elements with a matching class attribute. The dot is part of the selector:

<p class="lead">Fresh bread is baked every morning.</p>

.lead {
  font-size: 1.125rem;
  color: #444;
}

Classes can be reused on many elements. They are the main tool for component styles.

items.title: ID selectors
items.text:
An id selector targets one element:

<header id="site-header">...</header>

#site-header {
  background: #111;
  color: #fff;
}

An id must be unique on the page. Avoid using ids for routine styling because they have high specificity and are hard to override later. Use them for in-page links and JavaScript hooks.

items.title: Grouping selectors
items.text:
Apply the same declarations to several selectors with a comma:

h1,
h2,
h3 {
  font-weight: 600;
  line-height: 1.2;
}

items.title: Descendant and child selectors
items.text:
/* any <a> inside <nav> */
nav a {
  text-decoration: none;
}

/* only direct <li> children of <ul> */
ul > li {
  margin-bottom: 0.25rem;
}

The space is a descendant combinator. The > is a child combinator. Use the child combinator when you only want direct children.

items.title: Attribute selectors
items.text:
/* links that open in a new tab */
a[target="_blank"] {
  text-decoration: underline;
}

/* email inputs */
input[type="email"] {
  border-color: #888;
}

Attribute selectors are useful when the attribute itself carries meaning you want to style.

items.title: Choosing a selector
items.text:
• Use a class for a reusable visual style.
  • Use a type selector for base element styles.
  • Use an id for a unique anchor or script hook, not for routine styling.
  • Keep selectors short. body main article ul li a is a sign that the link needs a class.

Pseudo-classes such as :hover and pseudo-elements such as ::before have their own chapters.

items.title: Try it
items.text:
Add three links to a page: one normal link, one with class="nav-link", and one with target="_blank".

  1. Style all links with a type selector.
  2. Give .nav-link a different colour.
  3. Style a[target="_blank"] with an underline.
  4. Add a rule for nav a and check which links it affects.

Use the browser's inspector to see which rule wins.

Next: Nesting

items.title: Nesting
items.text:
CSS nesting lets you write a selector inside another rule. It keeps related styles together and mirrors the structure of your HTML.

Native CSS nesting is supported in current browsers. If you need to support an older browser, write the selectors separately.

items.title: Without nesting
items.text:
.card {
  padding: 1rem;
  border: 1px solid #ddd;
}

.card h2 {
  margin: 0 0 0.5rem;
}

.card p {
  color: #444;
}

.card a {
  text-decoration: none;
}

items.title: With nesting
items.text:
.card {
  padding: 1rem;
  border: 1px solid #ddd;

  h2 {
    margin: 0 0 0.5rem;
  }

  p {
    color: #444;
  }

  a {
    text-decoration: none;
  }
}

Both versions do the same thing. The nested version keeps the .card styles in one place.

items.title: The & selector
items.text:
& refers to the parent selector. Use it for states and modifiers:

.btn {
  padding: 0.5rem 1rem;
  background: #eee;

  &:hover {
    background: #ddd;
  }

  &:focus-visible {
    outline: 2px solid #333;
    outline-offset: 2px;
  }

  &.primary {
    background: #0a58ca;
    color: #fff;
  }
}

This compiles to .btn:hover, .btn:focus-visible, and .btn.primary.

items.title: Nesting media queries
items.text:
Media queries can also be nested:

.card {
  padding: 1rem;

  @media (min-width: 640px) {
    padding: 1.5rem;
  }
}

This keeps the responsive change next to the component it affects.

items.title: When not to nest
items.text:
Do not nest just because you can. Deep selectors are hard to override:

/* avoid */
.page .content .card .header h2 a {
  color: crimson;
}

Prefer a class on the target:

.card-title {
  color: crimson;
}

One level of nesting is usually enough. If you need three, add a class instead.

items.title: Try it
items.text:
Take a card component and write its styles without nesting. Then rewrite them with nesting.

  1. Put the card's own properties in the outer rule.
  2. Nest the h2, p, and a rules inside .card.
  3. Add &:hover and &:focus-visible states.
  4. Add a nested media query that changes the padding at 640px.

Open the page and check that the styles still apply. If they do not, confirm that the opening and closing braces match.

Next: The Cascade

items.title: The Cascade
items.text:
When several rules target the same element, the browser has to choose which declaration wins. That process is the cascade.

For everyday CSS, three things decide the result:

  1. Importance
  2. Specificity
  3. Source order

items.title: Source order
items.text:
If two rules have the same importance and specificity, the one that appears later wins:

p {
  color: #333;
}

p {
  color: crimson;
}

Every paragraph is crimson because the second rule comes later.

The same applies across stylesheets. A stylesheet linked later in <head> comes after one linked earlier. A <style> block comes after a linked stylesheet if it appears after the <link> element.

Put general rules first and overrides later:

/* base */
p {
  color: #333;
  line-height: 1.6;
}

/* later, same specificity, so this wins */
.lead {
  color: #111;
  font-size: 1.125rem;
}

Here .lead also has higher specificity than p, so it wins for elements with that class.

items.title: Importance
items.text:
!important makes a declaration beat normal declarations:

p {
  color: crimson !important;
}

Use it rarely. It is useful when you must override CSS you cannot edit, such as a third-party widget. If you need !important to beat your own stylesheet, your selectors are probably too specific or your source order is unclear.

items.title: Inline styles
items.text:
An inline style wins over normal rules in a stylesheet because it applies directly to the element:

<p style="color: crimson;">Hello</p>
