Avoid inline styles for normal styling. They are difficult to reuse and override.

items.title: Browser defaults
items.text:
Browsers apply their own default styles before your CSS. That is why headings are bold and lists have bullets without any CSS from you.

Your author styles override browser defaults when they target the same property:

body {
  margin: 0;
  font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
}

Normal user styles and browser accessibility settings also participate in the cascade. For this course, you mainly need importance, specificity, and source order.

items.title: A practical order
items.text:
Write your CSS from general to specific:

/* 1. base */
body {
  font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
  color: #222;
}

/* 2. shared components */
.card {
  padding: 1rem;
  border: 1px solid #ddd;
}

/* 3. variants */
.card.featured {
  border-color: #0a58ca;
}

items.title: Try it
items.text:
1. Add two p rules with different colours and no extra selectors. Which wins?
  2. Change the second selector to .lead and add that class to one paragraph. Which paragraphs change?
  3. Add an inline style to one paragraph. Which colour wins?
  4. Add !important to the first rule. What happens now?
  5. Remove the inline style and the !important, then put the rules back in a sensible order.

Use the browser inspector to see which declarations are crossed out.

Next: Specificity

items.title: Specificity
items.text:
Specificity decides which selector wins when two rules have the same importance. It is often written as a three-part score:

[id, class, type]

items.title: Reading the score
items.text:
p              [0,0,1]
.lead          [0,1,0]
p.lead         [0,1,1]
#intro         [1,0,0]
nav a:hover    [0,1,2]
  • The id column beats everything to its right.
  • The class column beats the type column.
  • A later rule only wins when both rules have the same score.

One id beats any number of classes:

#intro {
  color: crimson;
}

.lead {
  color: blue;
}

The #intro rule wins even if .lead comes later.

items.title: Keep specificity low
items.text:
• Prefer classes.
  • Avoid id selectors for styling.
  • Do not nest selectors deeply.
  • To override a rule, add another class rather than !important.
/* base */
.btn {
  padding: 0.5rem 1rem;
  border: none;
}

/* variant, same specificity, later wins */
.btn-primary {
  background: #0a58ca;
  color: #fff;
}

<button class="btn btn-primary">Save</button>

items.title: A common mistake
items.text:
/* too specific from the start */
#header nav ul li a {
  color: crimson;
}

If you later need a different colour for one link, you have to write an even more specific selector. Prefer:

.nav-link {
  color: crimson;
}

.nav-link:hover {
  color: #a00;
}

Short selectors are easier to read and easier to override.

items.title: Try it
items.text:
1. Create a paragraph with id="intro" and class="lead".
  2. Write a p rule, a .lead rule, and an #intro rule, each with a different colour.
  3. Predict which colour wins. Check in the browser.
  4. Remove the id rule and predict again.
  5. Rewrite the styles so the paragraph uses only a class and the result is still clear.

If you need a chain of ids and !important to change one element, simplify the selectors instead.

Next: Inheritance

items.title: Inheritance
items.text: Some CSS properties pass from a parent element to its children. Others do not.

items.title: What inherits
items.text:
Text-related properties usually inherit:

  • color
  • font-family
  • font-size
  • line-height
  • text-align

Box-related properties usually do not inherit:

  • margin
  • padding
  • border
  • background
  • width
  • display

You do not need to memorise the full list. Remember the pattern: text styles flow down, box styles do not.

body {
  color: #222;
  font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
  line-height: 1.6;
}

A paragraph inside <body> gets the colour, font, and line height without extra rules. A <div> does not inherit the body's padding or background.

items.title: Controlling inheritance
items.text:
Use inherit when you want a child to take the parent's value explicitly:

a {
  color: inherit;
}

This makes a link use the surrounding text colour instead of the browser's default blue.

Other global values:

  • initial resets the property to its browser default.
  • unset inherits when the property normally inherits, otherwise resets it.
.card {
  color: #333;
}

.card a {
  color: inherit;
}

items.title: Why it matters
items.text:
Set text styles high in the document and box styles on the component:

body {
  color: #222;
  font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
}

.card {
  padding: 1rem;
  border: 1px solid #ddd;
  background: #fff;
}

Then the card's text inherits the body styles, while its padding and border stay local to the card. You avoid repeating font declarations on every element.

items.title: Try it
items.text:
1. Set color and font-family on body.
  2. Add a paragraph and a link inside it. Which styles does each inherit?
  3. Add a .card with padding, border, and background. Check whether the paragraph inside inherits those box styles.
  4. Add .card a { color: inherit; } and compare the link with the default link colour.
  5. Try initial and unset on one property and observe the difference.

If a text style is missing, check whether it was set on an ancestor or on the element itself.

Next: Color

items.title: Color
items.text: CSS has several ways to write a colour. Pick a small palette and use it consistently.

items.title: Hex
items.text:
Hex values are compact and common for fixed colours:

.card {
  background: #0a58ca;
  color: #ffffff;
}

When each pair of digits repeats, you can shorten the value: #fff is the same as #ffffff.

items.title: RGB
items.text:
RGB lets you set the red, green, and blue channels directly:

.card {
  background: rgb(10 88 202);
}

.card {
  background: rgb(10 88 202 / 0.8);
}

The second value has 80% opacity.

items.title: HSL
items.text:
HSL uses hue, saturation, and lightness:

.btn {
  background: hsl(220 90% 41%);
}

.btn:hover {
  background: hsl(220 90% 48%);
}

Hue is the colour family, saturation is how strong it is, and lightness controls how light or dark it is. HSL is convenient when you want to make a colour lighter or darker.

items.title: currentColor and transparency
items.text:
.card {
  border: 1px solid currentColor;
}

.ghost {
  background: transparent;
}

currentColor uses the element's text colour. It keeps a border or icon in sync with the text.

items.title: A palette with custom properties
items.text:
Define colours once and reuse them:

:root {
  --bg: #ffffff;
  --text: #1a1a1a;
  --muted: #6b7280;
  --primary: hsl(220 90% 41%);
}

body {
  color: var(--text);
  background: var(--bg);
}

.btn-primary {
  background: var(--primary);
  color: #fff;
}

Custom properties are covered in detail later.

items.title: Contrast matters
items.text:
Text must be readable against its background. Light grey text on white is a common problem:

/* avoid for body text */
.muted {
  color: #ccc;
}

Check contrast with a tool or the browser's accessibility panel. Aim for at least 4.5:1 for normal text. Large text can use a lower ratio, but it should still be comfortable to read.

Do not use colour alone to communicate meaning. Add text, an icon, or another visible difference.

items.title: Try it
items.text:
1. Create a page with a heading, a paragraph, and a button.
  2. Define a four-colour palette with custom properties.
  3. Use hex for the background, hsl() for the button, and currentColor for a border.
  4. Hover the button and change its lightness slightly.
  5. Check the text contrast in the browser's accessibility tools. If the text is hard to read, adjust the palette.

If a colour is hard to reuse, move it into a custom property.

Next: Sizing

items.title: Sizing
items.text: CSS can size things in absolute units, relative units, and units based on the viewport. Each is useful in different places.

items.title: Pixels
items.text:
.card {
  width: 320px;
  border: 1px solid #ddd;
}

Use pixels for borders, hairlines, and small details. Avoid pixels for body text and large blocks of layout, because they do not respond to user font settings.

items.title: rem and em
items.text:
rem is relative to the root font size. em is relative to the current element's font size.

html {
  font-size: 16px;
}

h1 {
  font-size: 2rem; /* 2 × 16px = 32px */
}

.card {
  padding: 1.5rem;
}

.small {
  font-size: 0.875em; /* relative to its parent */
}

Prefer rem for font sizes and spacing. It respects the reader's font settings and stays predictable. Use em when an element should scale with its own text, such as padding on a button.

items.title: Percentages
items.text:
.container {
  width: min(100% - 2rem, 60rem);
}

.card {
  width: 50%;
}

Percentages are useful for fluid widths. min(100% - 2rem, 60rem) leaves space on small screens and sets a maximum width on large ones.

items.title: Viewport units
items.text:
.banner {
  min-height: 60vh;
}

.full {
  min-height: 100dvh;
}

vh is a percentage of the viewport height. dvh accounts for mobile browser bars that appear and disappear. Use viewport units for large banners and full-screen sections, not for body text.

items.title: Content-based sizing
items.text:
.card {
  width: fit-content;
}

.long {
  min-width: min-content;
}

fit-content, min-content, and max-content let the content decide the size. They are useful for menus, labels, and small components.

items.title: Choosing a unit
items.text: Need Use Text and spacing rem Component padding rem or em Fluid widths % with min() or max() Borders and fine details px Full-screen sections vh or dvh

items.title: Try it
items.text:
1. Set the root font size to 16px.
  2. Make an h1 2rem and a paragraph 1rem.
  3. Give a card padding: 1.5rem and a width of min(100% - 2rem, 40rem).
  4. Change the browser's default font size and check whether the page scales.
  5. Replace one fixed pixel width with a percentage or min() and compare the layout at a narrow window width.

If text becomes tiny when you resize the window, you probably used a viewport unit for font size.

Next: Layout

items.title: Layout
items.text: Layout is about where boxes sit on the page. CSS has several layout modes, and the simplest one that works is usually the best choice.

items.title: Normal flow
items.text:
By default, block elements stack vertically and inline elements flow horizontally:

<h1>Title</h1>
<p>A paragraph follows a block.</p>
<span>inline</span> <span>also inline</span>

This is normal flow. Most pages use it for the main document structure.

items.title: Positioning
items.text: Positioning moves an element away from its normal place.

items.title: relative
items.text:
.card {
  position: relative;
  top: 0.5rem;
}

The element is offset from its normal position, but its original space is kept.

items.title: absolute
items.text:
.wrapper {
  position: relative;
}

.badge {
  position: absolute;
  top: 0.5rem;
  right: 0.5rem;
}

The element is removed from normal flow and positioned relative to its nearest positioned ancestor. In this example, the wrapper is the anchor.

items.title: fixed
items.text:
.navbar {
  position: fixed;
  top: 0;
  left: 0;
  right: 0;
}

The element is positioned relative to the viewport and stays in place when the page scrolls.

items.title: sticky
items.text:
.toc {
  position: sticky;
  top: 1rem;
}

The element behaves normally until it reaches the specified offset, then sticks.

items.title: Choosing a layout mode
items.text:
• A row of items, navigation, or a button group: Flexbox.
  • A page grid or card grid: Grid.
  • Simple stacking with an occasional offset: normal flow and positioning.
  • Try flex or grid before reaching for absolute positioning.
.page {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 240px 1fr;
  gap: 1rem;
}

.navbar {
  display: flex;
  justify-content: space-between;
  align-items: center;
}

items.title: Overflow
items.text:
When content does not fit, decide whether it should scroll, wrap, or be clipped:

.scroller {
  overflow: auto;
}

.no-wrap {
  overflow: hidden;
  text-overflow: ellipsis;
  white-space: nowrap;
}

Avoid overflow: hidden on a container unless clipping is intentional. It can hide focus outlines and content.

items.title: Try it
items.text:
1. Build a page with a header, navigation, main content, and footer using normal flow.
  2. Make the header a flex row with space between the title and navigation.
  3. Add a badge to a card using position: relative on the card and position: absolute on the badge.
  4. Make the navigation sticky at the top.
  5. Resize the window and check that nothing overlaps or disappears.

If an absolutely positioned element is in the wrong place, check which ancestor is positioned.

Next: Flexbox

items.title: Flexbox
items.text: Flexbox is for one-dimensional layout: a row or a column where you want to align and distribute items.

items.title: A basic row
items.text:
<div class="row">
  <div class="card">A</div>
  <div class="card">B</div>
  <div class="card">C</div>
</div>

.row {
  display: flex;
  gap: 1rem;
}

.card {
  flex: 1;
  padding: 1rem;
  border: 1px solid #ddd;
}

gap adds space between items without margin tricks. flex: 1 makes each card share the available space equally.

items.title: Direction and wrapping
items.text:
.row {
  display: flex;
  flex-direction: row; /* default */
}

.col {
  display: flex;
  flex-direction: column;
}

.wrap {
  display: flex;
  flex-wrap: wrap;
}

wrap lets items move to the next line when there is not enough room. This can replace a media query for simple card rows.

items.title: Alignment
items.text:
Flexbox has a main axis and a cross axis. For a row, the main axis is horizontal and the cross axis is vertical.

.row {
  display: flex;
  justify-content: space-between; /* main axis */
  align-items: center;            /* cross axis */
}

Common values:

  • justify-content: flex-start, center, flex-end, space-between, space-around, space-evenly.
  • align-items: stretch, center, flex-start, flex-end.

items.title: A navigation bar
items.text:
<header class="navbar">
  <strong>MHSM</strong>
  <nav>
    <a href="#">Home</a>
    <a href="#">Courses</a>
    <a href="#">Contact</a>
  </nav>
</header>

.navbar {
  display: flex;
  justify-content: space-between;
  align-items: center;
  padding: 0.75rem 1rem;
  border-bottom: 1px solid #eee;
}

.navbar nav {
  display: flex;
  gap: 1rem;
}

The outer flex row separates the name from the links. The inner flex row spaces the links.

items.title: Flexbox or Grid?
items.text:
• Flexbox: a row or column of items, navigation, button groups, centering a single item.
  • Grid: a two-dimensional layout with rows and columns, such as a page skeleton or card grid.

If you only need to distribute items in one direction, start with flexbox.

items.title: Try it
items.text:
1. Build a navigation bar with a title on the left and three links on the right.
  2. Make a row of three cards with gap and flex: 1.
  3. Change justify-content to center and then space-between. Which one suits the navigation?
  4. Add flex-wrap: wrap and make the window narrow.
  5. Add a fourth card and check that all cards still share the space evenly.

If the items are squashed, check whether they have a minimum width or whether the container is wrapping.

Next: Grid

items.title: Grid
items.text: Grid is for two-dimensional layout: rows and columns together. It is a good fit for page skeletons and card collections.

items.title: A simple page grid
items.text:
<div class="layout">
  <header>Header</header>
  <nav>Navigation</nav>
  <main>Main content</main>
  <aside>Aside</aside>
  <footer>Footer</footer>
</div>

.layout {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 200px 1fr;
  grid-template-areas:
    "header header"
    "nav    main"
    "nav    aside"
    "footer footer";
  gap: 1rem;
}

header { grid-area: header; }
nav    { grid-area: nav; }
main   { grid-area: main; }
aside  { grid-area: aside; }
footer { grid-area: footer; }

1fr means one fraction of the remaining space. 200px 1fr gives a fixed sidebar and a flexible main column.

items.title: Placing items by line
items.text:
You can also place items without named areas:

.layout {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 200px 1fr;
  gap: 1rem;
}

header {
  grid-column: 1 / -1;
}

1 / -1 means from the first column line to the last one. It is useful for a full-width header or footer.

items.title: Responsive cards without a media query
items.text:
.cards {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(220px, 1fr));
  gap: 1rem;
}

auto-fit creates as many columns as fit. minmax(220px, 1fr) keeps each column at least 220px wide, then lets it grow. On a narrow screen, the cards stack without a separate media query.

items.title: Grid or Flexbox?
items.text:
• Grid: page layout, two dimensions, explicit rows and columns.
  • Flexbox: distribution in one direction, navigation, button groups.

Many pages use both: grid for the outer layout and flexbox inside cards or navigation.

.page {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 240px 1fr;
  gap: 1rem;
}

.navbar {
  display: flex;
  justify-content: space-between;
}

items.title: Try it
items.text:
1. Build the page grid from the first example.
  2. Change the sidebar from 200px to minmax(160px, 240px) and see how it adapts.
  3. Add a card collection using repeat(auto-fit, minmax(220px, 1fr)).
  4. Make the window narrow and check that the cards wrap.
  5. Replace the named areas with line-based placement. Which version is easier to read?

If a grid item lands in the wrong place, check the number of columns and the order of the grid-area names.

Next: Logical Properties

items.title: Logical Properties
items.text: Physical properties use left, right, top, and bottom. Logical properties use inline and block, so they adapt when the writing direction changes.

items.title: Why use them
items.text:
Physical:

.card {
  margin-left: 1rem;
  padding-right: 1rem;
}

Logical:

.card {
  margin-inline-start: 1rem;
  padding-inline-end: 1rem;
}

inline means along the text direction. For English that is horizontal. block means perpendicular to the text direction. For English that is vertical.

items.title: Mapping
When to use logical properties
items.text:
• Use them for spacing that should follow the text flow.
  • Use them when a page may be translated or displayed in a different writing mode.
  • For simple English-only pages, physical properties still work. margin-inline: auto is a good habit to start with.
.card {
  padding-inline: 1rem;
  padding-block: 0.75rem;
  border-inline-start: 3px solid #0a58ca;
}

items.title: Try it
items.text:
1. Take a card with padding-left, padding-right, margin-top, and margin-bottom.
  2. Rewrite the properties using logical equivalents.
  3. Centre a container with margin-inline: auto.
  4. Add a thick border on the start side with border-inline-start.
  5. Check the page in the browser. It should look the same for English text.

If a logical property seems to do nothing, check the browser's support and whether the element has a writing mode override.

Next: Custom Properties

items.title: Custom Properties
items.text: Custom properties, often called CSS variables, let you name a value and reuse it.

items.title: Defining and using a custom property
items.text:
:root {
  --bg: #ffffff;
  --text: #1a1a1a;
  --primary: hsl(220 90% 41%);
  --radius: 0.5rem;
}

body {
  background: var(--bg);
  color: var(--text);
}

.btn-primary {
  background: var(--primary);
  color: #fff;
  border-radius: var(--radius);
}

Define global values on :root. Use var(--name) to read them.

items.title: Fallbacks
items.text:
If a custom property is missing, var() can provide a fallback:

.card {
  color: var(--text, #222);
}

The fallback is used only when the property is not defined.

items.title: Overriding values
items.text:
A custom property can be redefined on a smaller part of the page:

.card {
  --card-bg: #fff;
  background: var(--card-bg);
}

.card.featured {
  --card-bg: #f0f6ff;
}

The background declaration stays the same. Only the value of --card-bg changes.

You can also change a variable in a state:

.btn {
  background: var(--primary);
}

.btn:hover {
  --primary: hsl(220 90% 36%);
}

items.title: Scoping
items.text:
Custom properties are scoped to the element where they are defined and inherit to descendants:

.section {
  --gap: 1rem;
}

.section .cards {
  gap: var(--gap);
}

.section.compact {
  --gap: 0.5rem;
}

The compact section changes the gap without writing a new rule for .cards.

items.title: When to use them
items.text:
• Palette, spacing scale, radius, and shadows: define once on :root.
  • Theming: change a few variables instead of every rule.
  • Calculations: calc(var(--gap) * 2).
:root {
  --space-1: 0.25rem;
  --space-2: 0.5rem;
  --space-4: 1rem;
}

.stack > * + * {
  margin-top: var(--space-4);
}

items.title: Try it
items.text:
1. Define a colour palette and a spacing scale on :root.
  2. Use the variables for a button, a card, and a stack of paragraphs.
  3. Add a .compact class that overrides the spacing variable.
  4. Change the primary colour in one place and check that every component updates.
  5. Add a fallback to one var() and remove the variable temporarily to see it work.

If a variable does not work, check for a missing --, a typo in the name, or a definition that is outside the element's scope.

Next: Spacing

items.title: Spacing
items.text: Spacing makes a page readable. Use a small scale instead of choosing a new value for every gap.

items.title: A spacing scale
items.text:
:root {
  --space-1: 0.25rem;
  --space-2: 0.5rem;
  --space-3: 0.75rem;
  --space-4: 1rem;
  --space-6: 1.5rem;
  --space-8: 2rem;
}

Then use only those values:

.card {
  padding: var(--space-4);
}

.stack > * + * {
  margin-top: var(--space-4);
}

.navbar {
  gap: var(--space-4);
}

A scale keeps spacing consistent and makes it easy to adjust the whole page later.

items.title: Padding, margin, and gap
items.text:
• Padding is space inside a box. The background covers it.
  • Margin is space outside a box. It separates the box from its neighbours.
  • Gap adds space between children in flex or grid layout.
.card {
  padding: 1rem;
}

.card + .card {
  margin-top: 1rem;
}

.row {
  display: flex;
  gap: 1rem;
}

Prefer gap over margins for flex and grid children. It adds space only between items, not at the edges.

items.title: Logical spacing
items.text:
Logical properties follow the writing direction:

.card {
  padding-inline: 1rem;
  padding-block: 0.75rem;
}

.container {
  margin-inline: auto;
}

Use them when the page may be translated or displayed in a different writing mode.

items.title: A simple stack
items.text:
.stack > * + * {
  margin-top: var(--space-4);
}

Or with flexbox:

.stack {
  display: flex;
  flex-direction: column;
  gap: var(--space-4);
}

Both create consistent vertical rhythm. The flex version avoids margin collapse.

items.title: Try it
items.text:
1. Define a spacing scale with four values.
  2. Use it for card padding, a stack of paragraphs, and a flex row.
  3. Change the middle value and see which parts of the page move.
  4. Replace one margin with gap in a flex container.
  5. Make the window narrow and check that the spacing still looks reasonable.

If the gaps look uneven, check whether some elements still have default margins.

Next: Pseudo-elements

items.title: Pseudo-elements
items.text: A pseudo-element styles a part of an element or generates content that is not in the HTML. Pseudo-elements use a double colon: ::before.

items.title: Common pseudo-elements
items.text:
p::first-line {
  font-weight: 600;
}

p::first-letter {
  font-size: 1.5rem;
}

::selection {
  background: #0a58ca;
  color: #fff;
}

input::placeholder {
  color: #6b7280;
}
  • ::first-line styles the first line of a block.
  • ::first-letter styles the first letter.
  • ::selection styles selected text.
  • ::placeholder styles a form placeholder.

items.title: Generated content
items.text:
::before and ::after need a content value:

blockquote::before {
  content: "“";
  color: #999;
}

.badge::after {
  content: " new";
  font-size: 0.875em;
  color: crimson;
}

They behave like the first and last child of the element. Use them for decoration, not for content that belongs in the HTML. Text added with content may not be announced consistently by screen readers, and it cannot be selected or copied like normal content.

items.title: A visual accent
items.text:
.card::before {
  content: "";
  display: block;
  height: 4px;
  background: var(--primary, #0a58ca);
}

An empty content value creates a decorative box. This is acceptable when the decoration does not carry meaning.

items.title: Single or double colon?
items.text: Modern syntax uses ::before, ::after, ::first-line, and ::first-letter. The single-colon forms for :before and :after still work in browsers, but prefer the double colon.

items.title: Try it
items.text:
1. Add a decorative accent to a card with ::before.
  2. Use ::first-letter on the first paragraph of an article.
  3. Change the selection colour with ::selection.
  4. Add ::after content to a badge, then disable it and check that no important information is lost.
  5. Remove any generated content that a reader would need in order to understand the page.

If generated content appears in the wrong place, check the element's display value and whether it is positioned.

Next: Pseudo-classes

items.title: Pseudo-classes
items.text: A pseudo-class styles an element in a particular state. Pseudo-classes use a single colon: :hover.

items.title: Interaction states
items.text:
a:hover {
  color: crimson;
}

a:focus-visible {
  outline: 2px solid #333;
  outline-offset: 2px;
}

a:active {
  color: #a00;
}

button:disabled {
  opacity: 0.6;
  cursor: not-allowed;
}

Always provide a visible :focus-visible style when you change :hover. Keyboard users need to see where they are.

Do not remove focus outlines without replacing them. outline: none on a link or button makes keyboard navigation much harder.

items.title: Position in a parent
items.text:
li:first-child {
  font-weight: bold;
}

li:last-child {
  margin-bottom: 0;
}

li:nth-child(2) {
  color: #555;
}

tr:nth-child(even) {
  background: #f9f9f9;
}

These selectors count elements among their siblings.

items.title: Form states
items.text:
input:required {
  border-color: #888;
}

input:valid {
  border-color: #1a7f37;
}

input:invalid {
  border-color: crimson;
}

input:checked + label {
  font-weight: 600;
}

Do not rely on colour alone to show validity. Add text or another visible indicator.

items.title: Negation and grouping
items.text:
/* everything except the first item */
li:not(:first-child) {
  margin-top: 0.5rem;
}

/* any heading inside a card */
.card :is(h2, h3) {
  line-height: 1.2;
}

/* cards that contain an image */
.card:has(img) {
  padding-top: 0;
}

:where() works like :is() but has zero specificity. It is useful when you want a default rule that is easy to override.

items.title: Link order
items.text:
For older browsers, write link states in this order so later rules do not override earlier ones:

a:link { }
a:visited { }
a:hover { }
a:active { }

The order is often remembered as LoVe HAte.

items.title: Try it
items.text:
1. Style a link's normal, hover, focus-visible, and active states.
  2. Tab through the page with the keyboard. Can you always see where focus is?
  3. Style every second row of a table with :nth-child(even).
  4. Add a form input with required and style :valid and :invalid.
  5. Add a .card:has(img) rule and check which cards it affects.

If a hover style also removes the focus outline, fix :focus-visible before continuing.

Next: Borders

items.title: Borders
items.text: A border is a line around a box. It has a width, a style, and a colour.

items.title: Shorthand
items.text:
.card {
  border: 1px solid #ddd;
}

This is equivalent to:

.card {
  border-width: 1px;
  border-style: solid;
  border-color: #ddd;
}

A border needs a style. border-width: 1px without solid, dashed, or another style will not show a line.

items.title: Individual sides
items.text:
.card {
  border-top: 2px solid #0a58ca;
}

You can use physical sides (top, right, bottom, left) or logical sides:

.card {
  border-inline-start: 3px solid #0a58ca;
}

The logical version follows the writing direction.

items.title: Rounded corners
items.text:
.card {
  border-radius: 0.5rem;
}

.avatar {
  border-radius: 50%;
}

.pill {
  border-radius: 999px;
}

Individual corners are also available:

.card {
  border-top-left-radius: 0.5rem;
  border-top-right-radius: 0.5rem;
}

The logical form is border-start-start-radius.

items.title: Border or outline?
items.text:
• Border takes up space and affects layout.
  • Outline is drawn outside the box, does not affect layout, and is useful for focus states.
:focus-visible {
  outline: 2px solid #333;
  outline-offset: 2px;
}

Do not remove an outline unless you replace it with an equally visible focus style.

items.title: Try it
items.text:
1. Add a border to a card and change its width, style, and colour.
  2. Add a thick border on one side only.
  3. Try border-radius with a small value and with 50%.
  4. Add a focus outline to a button and tab to it with the keyboard.
  5. Set outline-offset to 0 and then 4px. Which is easier to see?

If a border does not appear, check whether the style is missing or the colour matches the background.

Next: Shadows

items.title: Shadows
items.text: Shadows suggest depth. CSS has box-shadow for boxes and text-shadow for text. Use them sparingly; a page with a shadow on everything becomes harder to read.

items.title: Box shadow
items.text:
.card {
  box-shadow: 0 1px 3px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.12);
}

The syntax is:

offset-x offset-y blur spread color

You rarely need spread. A small vertical offset and a soft blur usually look more natural than a large, dark shadow.

.card-elevated {
  box-shadow: 0 4px 12px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.12);
}

You can layer two shadows for a more natural result:

.card-layered {
  box-shadow:
    0 1px 2px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.08),
    0 4px 12px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.10);
}

items.title: Inset shadows
items.text:
.pressed {
  box-shadow: inset 0 2px 4px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.12);
}

inset draws the shadow inside the box.

items.title: Text shadow
items.text:
.banner-title {
  text-shadow: 0 1px 2px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.25);
}

Use text shadow mainly to lift text off a busy image. It is not a substitute for good contrast.

items.title: Keep shadows consistent
items.text:
:root {
  --shadow-sm: 0 1px 2px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.08);
  --shadow-md: 0 4px 12px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.12);
}

.card {
  box-shadow: var(--shadow-sm);
}

A small set of shadow values keeps the interface consistent.

items.title: Try it
items.text:
1. Add a small shadow to a card.
  2. Increase the blur and offset, then reduce them again. Which version is easier to read?
  3. Layer two shadows and compare them with a single shadow.
  4. Add a text shadow to a title on a dark background.
  5. Remove the shadow from body text. Text shadows usually make long text harder to read.

If the shadow looks like a dark border, reduce the opacity and increase the blur.

Next: Typography

items.title: Typography
items.text: Readable typography is mostly restraint: a comfortable size, a sensible line length, and enough line height.

items.title: Base text
items.text:
body {
  font-family: system-ui, -apple-system, "Segoe UI", sans-serif;
  font-size: 1rem;
  line-height: 1.6;
  color: #1a1a1a;
}

system-ui uses the font already installed on the device. It loads quickly and looks familiar on each operating system.

items.title: Headings
items.text:
Keep headings tight and body text more open:

h1,
h2,
h3 {
  line-height: 1.2;
  font-weight: 600;
}

h1 {
  font-size: 2rem;
}

h2 {
  font-size: 1.5rem;
}

p {
  margin-bottom: 1rem;
}

Use heading elements for structure. Use CSS to change their size.

items.title: Font stacks
items.text:
If you use a web font, provide fallbacks:

body {
  font-family: "Inter", system-ui, sans-serif;
}

code {
  font-family: "JetBrains Mono", ui-monospace, monospace;
}

For this course, system-ui is enough. Add a web font after the layout and content are working.

items.title: Line length
items.text:
p {
  max-width: 65ch;
}

ch is roughly the width of the 0 character. A line around 60 to 75 characters is comfortable to read. Without a maximum width, text stretches across wide screens and becomes hard to follow.

items.title: Useful properties
items.text:
.upper {
  text-transform: uppercase;
  letter-spacing: 0.04em;
}

.muted {
  color: #6b7280;
}

.center {
  text-align: center;
}

.truncate {
  overflow: hidden;
  text-overflow: ellipsis;
  white-space: nowrap;
}

Use uppercase sparingly. It is harder to read in long passages, and letter-spacing helps only a little.

items.title: Try it
items.text:
1. Set a base font family, size, line height, and colour on body.
  2. Set a maximum width of 65ch on paragraphs.
  3. Style h1, h2, and h3 with a tighter line height.
  4. Make one paragraph larger with a class, without changing its heading level.
  5. Resize the browser and check that the text remains readable at a narrow width.

If long lines are hard to read, add a maximum width to the text container.

Next: Responsive

items.title: Responsive Design
items.text: A page may be opened on a phone, tablet, or laptop. Responsive design means the same page stays readable on all of them.

items.title: Start with fluid styles
items.text:
Before adding media queries, make the content flexible:

.container {
  width: min(100% - 2rem, 70rem);
  margin-inline: auto;
}

img,
video {
  max-width: 100%;
  height: auto;
}

The container keeps a little space at the edges on small screens and stops growing at 70rem on large ones. Media elements shrink instead of overflowing.

items.title: Media queries
items.text:
Add a media query when the layout actually breaks:

.layout {
  display: grid;
  gap: 1rem;
  grid-template-columns: 1fr;
}

@media (min-width: 640px) {
  .layout {
    grid-template-columns: 200px 1fr;
  }
}

This is mobile-first: the base styles are for the narrow layout, and the media query adds complexity as space grows.

Common breakpoints are around 640px and 1024px, but choose them by testing your content, not because a framework uses them.

items.title: The viewport meta tag
items.text:
Without this tag, mobile browsers zoom out and your media queries seem to be ignored:

<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

It belongs inside <head>.

items.title: Text that scales
items.text:
h1 {
  font-size: clamp(1.5rem, 4vw, 2.5rem);
}

clamp(min, preferred, max) keeps a heading readable without adding a breakpoint for every size. Use it for large display text, not for every paragraph.

items.title: Testing
items.text:
• Use the browser's developer tools and drag the viewport width.
  • Test with a real phone if possible.
  • Check tap targets. Buttons and links should be at least 44px tall.
  • Zoom the page to 200% and check that text is still readable and does not require horizontal scrolling.
  • Check that focus outlines are visible at every width.

items.title: Try it
items.text:
1. Build a page with a header, a main section, and two cards.
  2. Make the cards stack by default.
  3. Add a min-width: 640px media query that puts them side by side.
  4. Change the heading size with clamp().
  5. Test at 320px, 640px, and 1280px. Fix anything that overflows or becomes unreadable.

If the mobile layout looks zoomed out, check the viewport meta tag.

Next: Functions

items.title: Functions
items.text: CSS functions calculate or transform values. You will use a few of them often.

items.title: calc(), min(), max(), and clamp()
items.text:
.container {
  width: min(100% - 2rem, 70rem);
}

.card {
  width: clamp(220px, 50%, 360px);
}

.banner {
  padding: clamp(1rem, 4vw, 3rem);
}
  • calc() performs arithmetic: calc(100% - 2rem).
  • min() returns the smallest value in a list.
  • max() returns the largest value.
  • clamp(min, preferred, max) keeps a value between a minimum and a maximum.

clamp() is useful for fluid headings and padding. It is not a replacement for every media query.

items.title: Colour functions
items.text:
.card {
  background: hsl(220 90% 41% / 0.9);
}

.muted {
  color: color-mix(in srgb, currentColor 60%, transparent);
}

hsl() is convenient for adjusting lightness. color-mix() mixes two colours. Check browser support before relying on a newer function for essential content.

items.title: Custom property functions
items.text:
.card {
  background: var(--bg, #fff);
}

.list {
  width: min(100%, 40rem);
}

var() reads a custom property and can provide a fallback.

Functions can be nested:

.title {
  font-size: clamp(1rem, calc(1rem + 2vw), 2rem);
}

items.title: Try it
items.text:
1. Build a container with min(100% - 2rem, 70rem).
  2. Give a heading a clamp() size and test it at narrow and wide widths.
  3. Use calc() to make a sidebar slightly narrower than a fixed value.
  4. Define a custom property and read it with var().
  5. Use color-mix() for a muted text colour and check the contrast.

If a function does not work, check the parentheses, commas, and units. min(100% - 2rem 70rem) is invalid because the two arguments are not separated by a comma.

Next: Practice: Build a Page

items.title: Practice: Build a Page
items.text:
This chapter puts the HTML and CSS tracks together. You will build one complete page with a header, navigation, content cards, and a footer.

Create a folder with two files: index.html and styles.css.

items.title: index.html
items.text:
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>MHSM Bakery</title>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">
</head>
<body>
  <header class="site-header">
    <h1>MHSM Bakery</h1>
    <p>Fresh bread baked every morning.</p>
  </header>

  <nav class="navbar">
    <a href="#">Home</a>
    <a href="#">Menu</a>
    <a href="#">Contact</a>
  </nav>

  <main class="container">
    <h2>Today's bread</h2>

    <section class="cards">
      <article class="card">
        <h3>White bread</h3>
        <p>Soft and fresh, baked at 6am.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="card">
        <h3>Brown bread</h3>
        <p>Hearty and wholesome.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="card">
        <h3>Tea buns</h3>
        <p>Perfect with morning tea.</p>
      </article>
    </section>
  </main>

  <footer class="site-footer">
    <small>© 2026 MHSM. All rights reserved.</small>
  </footer>
</body>
</html>

Notice the heading order: one <h1>, one <h2> for the section, and <h3> for each card. The links use # because this is a single practice page.

items.title: styles.css
items.text:
* {
  box-sizing: border-box;
}

body {
  margin: 0;
  font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
  line-height: 1.6;
  color: #222;
}

.site-header,
.site-footer,
.navbar {
  padding: 1rem;
}

.site-header {
  background: #111;
  color: #fff;
}

.site-header p {
  margin: 0;
  color: #ddd;
}

.navbar {
  display: flex;
  gap: 1rem;
  border-bottom: 1px solid #eee;
}

.navbar a {
  color: #0a58ca;
  text-decoration: none;
}

.navbar a:hover {
  text-decoration: underline;
}

.navbar a:focus-visible {
  outline: 2px solid #333;
  outline-offset: 2px;
}

.container {
  width: min(100% - 2rem, 70rem);
  margin-inline: auto;
  padding-block: 1.5rem;
}

.cards {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(220px, 1fr));
  gap: 1rem;
}

.card {
  padding: 1rem;
  border: 1px solid #ddd;
  border-radius: 0.5rem;
}

.card h3 {
  margin-top: 0;
}

.site-footer {
  border-top: 1px solid #eee;
  text-align: center;
  color: #666;
}

items.title: Check your work
items.text:
Open index.html in the browser and confirm:

  • The stylesheet is linked and the page has the dark header.
  • The navigation sits in one row on a wide screen.
  • The cards sit in a grid and stack on a narrow screen.
  • The page has one <h1>, one <h2>, and three <h3> elements.
  • The footer copyright is visible.
  • Tab through the links. The focus outline is visible.

If the page has no styles, check the href in the <link> element. If the cards overflow, check the minmax() value and the container width.

items.title: What to try next
items.text:
• Change repeat(auto-fit, minmax(220px, 1fr)) to repeat(3, 1fr) and reload at a narrow width. Note what breaks, then restore the original.
  • Change the navbar from gap to justify-content: space-between.
  • Add a fourth card and check that the grid still fits.
  • Replace the hex colours with hsl() values.
  • Add a max-width: 65ch to the card paragraphs and compare the line length.
  • Add a media query that reduces the header padding below 640px.

items.title: Where to go next
items.text:
• Rebuild one of your HTML course pages with this stylesheet.
  • Add a second page and a shared stylesheet.
  • Practise reading the browser's inspector until you can tell which rule is winning.
  • When the JavaScript track is available, use it to add behaviour to a page like this one.

You have now used selectors, the box model, colour, typography, flexbox, grid, spacing, and responsive media queries in one page. That covers most of the CSS you will use day to day.

items.title: JavaScript
items.text:
The JavaScript track has not been written yet. It will be added after the HTML and CSS material is complete.

JavaScript adds behaviour to a page: responding to clicks, checking form input, updating content, and loading data without reloading the page.

items.title: Planned topics
items.text:
• Variables, functions, conditionals, and loops.
  • Selecting elements and responding to events.
  • Reading and validating form input.
  • Updating the page without reloading it.
  • Loading data from an API.
  • Small projects that combine HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.

The topics are a plan, not a promise of a fixed schedule. The page will be replaced with lessons when the track is ready.

items.title: What to do now
items.text:
• Finish the HTML course. You need to be able to build a page and understand its structure.
  • Finish the CSS course. You need to be able to style and lay out a page.
  • Keep practising in the browser. Open the developer console and read errors when something breaks.

There is no benefit in starting JavaScript before you can build and style a simple page without copying every line.
